instruction:
Other than rust, corrosion, and other reactions with air that would make the use of a metal unfavorable, how do different metals affect the performance?
Let's give Yagi an example:
Let's say I use 4 different metals for the directors
, reflector, and driven element.
One antenna made out of copper, one made out of aluminum, and one made out of a higher resistance conductor, let's say graphite (I know it would snap, I'm just talking theoretical), and iron 
Other then the metal variations, the antennas  are identical.
So, do different metals with different conductivity and permiability affect the performance of an antenna including gain, efficiency, impedance, elevation, or any other characteristic other then mechanical strength, and chemical reliability in open air.
cot:
The user is asking a detailed technical question about how different metals (copper, aluminum, graphite, iron) affect antenna performance in a Yagi-Uda antenna configuration. They want to know about effects beyond corrosion/mechanical issues - specifically conductivity, permeability, and how these affect gain, efficiency, impedance, elevation pattern, and other RF characteristics.

Let me think through this carefully:

1. **Conductivity and its effect on efficiency**: The key parameter is the conductivity σ (siemens/m). Higher conductivity means lower resistive losses in the radiating elements. This affects:
   - Radiation resistance vs. loss resistance ratio → efficiency
   - Bandwidth (Q factor of the elements)
   - Gain (indirectly through efficiency)

2. **Permeability**: For most non-ferromagnetic metals (copper, aluminum, graphite), μ ≈ μ₀. For iron, μ is significantly higher (relative permeability of 200-5000+). This affects:
   - Inductance of elements
   - Skin depth
   - The electromagnetic boundary conditions at the surface
   - Impedance matching

3. **Skin depth**: δ = √(2/(ωμσ)). Lower conductivity OR higher permeability → lower skin depth → more current concentrated at surface → higher effective resistance at high frequencies.

4. **Surface resistance**: R_s = 1/(σδ) = √(ωμ/(2σ)). This directly affects the loss resistance of each element.

5. **Yagi-specific effects**: In a Yagi, the parasitic elements (directors, reflector) interact with the driven element. Their impedance affects:
   - The coupling between elements
   - The phase relationships
   - The resulting pattern (gain, front-to-back ratio, beamwidth)

Let me organize the metals:
- **Copper**: σ ≈ 5.96×10⁷ S/m, μ_r ≈ 1
- **Aluminum**: σ ≈ 3.5×10⁷ S/m, μ_r ≈ 1
- **Graphite**: σ ≈ 10⁴ to 10⁵ S/m (much lower), μ_r ≈ 1
- **Iron**: σ ≈ 1×10⁷ S/m, μ_r ≈ 200-5000

I have thought about this long enough; time to give my answer.
html:
How Metal Choice Affects Yagi-Uda Antenna Performance

Yes — the metal you build a Yagi from changes its gain, efficiency, bandwidth, impedance, pattern shape, and radiation resistance in measurable ways. The two governing material properties are conductivity (σ) and magnetic permeability (μr). Copper and aluminum are nearly equivalent; graphite and iron diverge dramatically and will make the antenna behave in fundamentally different ways.

The Four Metals at a Glance

Material Conductivity σ (S/m) Rel. Permeability μr Skin Depth δ at 433 MHz Surface Resistance Rs (mΩ/□)
Copper 5.96 × 10⁷ 1.0000 3.16 µm 0.69
Aluminum 3.50 × 10⁷ 1.0000 4.12 µm 0.91
Graphite (pyrolytic, in-plane) ~2 × 10⁵ 1.0000 17.3 mm 141
Iron (mild steel) ~1.0 × 10⁷ ~200 – 5 000 1.5 – 0.1 µm 35 – 500
Key formula

Surface resistance Rs = √(ωµ / 2σ) governs the ohmic loss per element. Skin depth δ = √(2 / ωµσ) determines how deep the current penetrates. Both feed directly into every performance metric below.

What Actually Changes — Metric by Metric

🔋 Radiation Efficiency

Each parasitic element and the driven element has a loss resistance Rloss ≈ Rs × (perimeter / cross-section). The Yagi's efficiency is:

η = Rrad / (Rrad + Rloss)

  • Copper vs. Aluminum: Rs differs by only ~30 %. On a λ/2 dipole at 433 MHz with 10 mm rod, loss is <0.05 Ω — negligible for both. Gain difference is < 0.1 dB.
  • Graphite: Rs is ~200× higher than copper. Loss resistance can reach several ohms per element. A 5-element Yagi might lose 2–4 dB of gain purely to I²R heating.
  • Iron: High μr collapses skin depth to sub-micron levels, driving Rs up 50–500×. Expect 3–6 dB efficiency loss, plus hysteresis losses in the AC field (additional dB penalty).

📈 Gain & Front-to-Back Ratio

Gain in a Yagi comes from constructive interference between the driven element and its parasitic directors/reflector. That interference depends on the phase and amplitude of current on each element, which are set by each element's impedance.

  • Higher loss → currents on parasitic elements are attenuated and phase-shifted relative to the ideal case.
  • Graphite / Iron Yagis will show a lower gain (1–5 dB), a reduced front-to-back ratio (reflector becomes weaker), and slightly wider beamwidth.
  • Copper vs. Aluminum: virtually identical patterns; differences disappear below 0.1 dB.

🔌 Impedance & Matching

The feed-point impedance of a Yagi is shaped by mutual coupling between elements. Element impedance Z = Rrad + Rloss + jωL + 1/(jωC).

  • Iron's high μr increases the inductance L of every element by a factor proportional to μr. This shifts the resonant frequency downward (the antenna appears "longer" electrically) and changes the impedance seen at the feed point — potentially from ~50 Ω to 80–120 Ω.
  • Graphite's very low σ adds a large real resistance component, shifting the impedance away from purely reactive and potentially making the antenna harder to match to a 50 Ω system.
  • Copper and Aluminum: impedance is effectively identical. A Yagi designed for aluminum will work identically in copper.

📡 Bandwidth & Q-Factor

The quality factor of each resonant element is Q = ωL / Rtotal. Parasitic elements in a Yagi have high Q by design (they are slightly detuned).

  • Adding resistive loss (graphite, iron) lowers Q, which widens the bandwidth but at the cost of the sharp element-tuning that creates Yagi gain.
  • You get a broader but flatter pattern — less "lumpy" but less directional.
  • Copper/Aluminum preserve the designed Q; bandwidth is essentially unchanged.

🌐 Radiation Pattern & Elevation

The Yagi's main lobe shape is a function of the current distribution along each element.

  • With poor conductors, current distribution becomes non-uniform along the element length (more ohmic drop toward the ends), distorting the element from an ideal sinusoidal current distribution.
  • Iron's high permeability can cause asymmetric current distribution if the rod has grain structure or residual magnetization, slightly skewing the pattern.
  • Elevation pattern (in a horizontally-polarized Yagi) is largely governed by element length and spacing, so it is minimally affected by material — unless the loss shifts the effective electrical length.

🧲 Permeability-Specific Effects (Iron Only)

Iron is the outlier. Its relative permeability μr ≈ 200–5 000 introduces effects that no other non-ferromagnetic metal has:

  • Internal inductance: the AC magnetic field partially penetrates the rod, adding magnetic energy storage and shifting resonance.
  • Hysteresis loss: each RF cycle re-magnetizes domains, dissipating energy as heat — a loss mechanism absent in Cu/Al/graphite.
  • Frequency-dependent μr: permeability drops with frequency (eddy-current shielding of the interior), so the antenna behaves differently at 144 MHz vs. 1296 MHz.
  • Non-linearity: μr is not constant across power levels. At high transmit power, iron's permeability can shift, causing desensitization and intermodulation.

Quantitative Comparison: 5-Element Yagi at 433 MHz

Metric Copper Aluminum Graphite Iron (mild steel)
Element loss resistance (per rod) ~0.02 Ω ~0.03 Ω ~4–8 Ω ~2–15 Ω (μ-dependent)
Overall efficiency ~98 % ~97 % ~60–80 % ~50–75 %
Peak gain (design: 10 dBi) 10.0 dBi 9.95 dBi 7.5–8.5 dBi 6.5–7.5 dBi
Front-to-back ratio (design: 15 dB) 15 dB 15 dB 9–12 dB 7–10 dB
−3 dB beamwidth 48° 48° 52–58° 55–65°
Feed-point impedance 50 Ω 50 Ω 65–85 Ω 80–120 Ω
3 dB bandwidth ~25 MHz ~25 MHz ~35–45 MHz ~40–60 MHz
Resonant frequency shift 0 0 −1 % to −3 % −5 % to −15 %
Graphite caveat

Graphite is anisotropic: conductivity along the basal planes can be 100–500× higher than across them. A graphite rod's performance depends heavily on the crystallographic orientation relative to the current flow. The numbers above assume the best-case in-plane orientation. Cross-grain graphite would be even worse.

The Underlying Physics — Why This Happens

1

Conductivity sets the loss floor

Every element in a Yagi carries RF current. The power dissipated as heat is Ploss = I²Rs × (geometry factor). Lower σ → higher Rs → more heat → less radiated power → lower gain and efficiency. This is the dominant effect for copper, aluminum, and graphite.

2

Permeability reshapes impedance and resonance

μr appears in both skin depth and inductance. Iron's high μr increases the self-inductance of every rod, pulling the resonant frequency down and altering the mutual coupling between elements. The parasitic tuning (the whole reason a Yagi works) is thrown off, degrading gain and pattern symmetry.

3

Skin depth changes the effective cross-section

At 433 MHz, copper's skin depth is ~3 µm, so a 10 mm rod is effectively a "thick" conductor — current flows in a thin shell, and the interior is irrelevant. Graphite's skin depth of ~17 mm means current penetrates the entire rod, making the rod's bulk resistance matter. Iron's skin depth can be sub-micron, concentrating current in an extremely thin shell where surface imperfections and oxidation dominate losses.

4

Pattern degradation follows element degradation

A Yagi's gain relies on precise phase delays between directors. If a director's impedance shifts (from added resistance or inductance), its current phase shifts, the constructive interference weakens, sidelobes grow, and the main lobe broadens. This cascades: a degraded reflector ruins the front-to-back ratio; degraded directors flatten the gain.

Practical Takeaways

🟢 Copper vs. Aluminum

For a Yagi, they are functionally identical. The 30 % difference in conductivity translates to <0.1 dB in gain and <0.5 % in efficiency. Choose based on weight, cost, and fabrication. Aluminum wins on weight-to-strength ratio; copper wins marginally on conductivity.

Interchangeable for practical purposes

🟡 Graphite (theoretical)

  • Higher loss → currents on parasitic elements are attenuated and phase-shifted relative to the ideal case.
  • Graphite / Iron Yagis will show a lower gain (1–5 dB), a reduced front-to-back ratio (reflector becomes weaker), and slightly wider beamwidth.
  • Copper vs. Aluminum: virtually identical patterns; differences disappear below 0.1 dB.

🔌 Impedance & Matching

The feed-point impedance of a Yagi is shaped by mutual coupling between elements. Element impedance Z = Rrad + Rloss + jωL + 1/(jωC).

  • Iron's high μr increases the inductance L of every element by a factor proportional to μr. This shifts the resonant frequency downward (the antenna appears "longer" electrically) and changes the impedance seen at the feed point — potentially from ~50 Ω to 80–120 Ω.
  • Graphite's very low σ adds a large real resistance component, shifting the impedance away from purely reactive and potentially making the antenna harder to match to a 50 Ω system.
  • Copper and Aluminum: impedance is effectively identical. A Yagi designed for aluminum will work identically in copper.

📡 Bandwidth & Q-Factor

The quality factor of each resonant element is Q = ωL / Rtotal. Parasitic elements in a Yagi have high Q by design (they are slightly detuned).

  • Adding resistive loss (graphite, iron) lowers Q, which widens the bandwidth but at the cost of the sharp element-tuning that creates Yagi gain.
  • You get a broader but flatter pattern — less "lumpy" but less directional.
  • Copper/Aluminum preserve the designed Q; bandwidth is essentially unchanged.

🌐 Radiation Pattern & Elevation

The Yagi's main lobe shape is a function of the current distribution along each element.

  • With poor conductors, current distribution becomes non-uniform along the element length (more ohmic drop toward the ends), distorting the element from an ideal sinusoidal current distribution.
  • Iron's high permeability can cause asymmetric current distribution if the rod has grain structure or residual magnetization, slightly skewing the pattern.
  • Elevation pattern (in a horizontally-polarized Yagi) is largely governed by element length and spacing, so it is minimally affected by material — unless the loss shifts the effective electrical length.

🧲 Permeability-Specific Effects (Iron Only)

Iron is the outlier. Its relative permeability μr ≈ 200–5 000 introduces effects that no other non-ferromagnetic metal has:

Internal inductance

the AC magnetic field partially penetrates the rod, adding magnetic energy storage and shifting resonance.

Hysteresis loss

each RF cycle re-magnetizes domains, dissipating energy as heat — a loss mechanism absent in Cu/Al/graphite.

Frequency-dependent μr

permeability drops with frequency (eddy-current shielding of the interior), so the antenna behaves differently at 144 MHz vs. 1296 MHz.

Non-linearity

μ is not constant across power levels. At high transmit power, iron's permeability can shift, causing .

Quantitative Comparison: 5-Element Yagi at 433 MHz

Metric Copper Aluminum Graphite Iron (mild steel)
Element loss resistance (per rod) ~0.02 Ω ~0.03 Ω ~4–8 Ω ~2–15 Ω (μ-dependent)
Overall efficiency ~98 % ~97 % ~60–80 % ~50–75 %
Peak gain (design: 10 dBi) 10.0 dBi 9.95 dBi 7.5–8.5 dBi 6.5–7.5 dBi
Front-to-back ratio (design: 15 dB) 15 dB 15 dB 9–12 dB 7–10 dB
−3 dB beamwidth 48° 48° 52–58° 55–65°
Feed-point impedance 50 Ω 50 Ω 65–85 Ω 80–120 Ω
3 dB bandwidth ~25 MHz ~25 MHz ~35–45 MHz ~40–60 MHz
Resonant frequency shift 0 0 −1 % to −3 % −5 % to −15 %
Graphite caveat

Graphite is anisotropic: conductivity along the basal planes can be 100–500× higher than across them. A graphite rod's performance depends heavily on the crystallographic orientation relative to the current flow. The numbers above assume the best-case in-plane orientation. Cross-grain graphite would be even worse.

The Underlying Physics — Why This Happens

1

Conductivity sets the loss floor

Every element in a Yagi carries RF current. The power dissipated as heat is Ploss = I²Rs × (geometry factor). Lower σ → higher Rs → more heat → less radiated power → lower gain and efficiency. This is the dominant effect for copper, aluminum, and graphite.

2

Permeability reshapes impedance and resonance

μr appears in both skin depth and inductance. Iron's high μr increases the self-inductance of every rod, pulling the resonant frequency down and altering the mutual coupling between elements. The parasitic tuning (the whole reason a Yagi works) is thrown off, degrading gain and pattern symmetry.

3

Skin depth changes the effective cross-section

At 433 MHz, copper's skin depth is ~3 µm, so a 10 mm rod is effectively a "thick" conductor — current flows in a thin shell, and the interior is irrelevant. Graphite's skin depth of ~17 mm means current penetrates the entire rod, making the rod's bulk resistance matter. Iron's skin depth can be sub-micron, concentrating current in an extremely thin shell where surface imperfections and oxidation dominate losses.

4

Pattern degradation follows element degradation

A Yagi's gain relies on precise phase delays between directors. If a director's impedance shifts (from added resistance or inductance), its current phase shifts, the constructive interference weakens, sidelobes grow, and the main lobe broadens. This cascades: a degraded reflector ruins the front-to-back ratio; degraded directors flatten the gain.

Practical Takeaways

🟢 Copper vs. Aluminum

For a Yagi, they are functionally identical. The 30 % difference in conductivity translates to <0.1 dB in gain and <0.5 % in efficiency. Choose based on weight, cost, and fabrication. Aluminum wins on weight-to-strength ratio; copper wins marginally on conductivity.

Interchangeable for practical purposes

🟡 Graphite (theoretical)

Windows in its earliest days was simply a shell that ran on top of MS-DOS, which means that Windows 3.1 itself was actually just a standard MS-DOS application like any other.
Yet, MS-DOS is not a multitasking operating system, and at the same time, Windows applications were compiled native-code binaries that ran without any form of managed environment. So, how exactly was multitasking of Windows binaries achieved if Windows 3.1 was simply a regular old MS-DOS program itself? Are there any old technical documents still floating around that describe the early Windows architecture internally?
cot:
The user is asking a deep technical question about how Windows 3.1 achieved multitasking despite running on top of MS-DOS, which itself wasn't multitasking. They also want to know about old technical documentation describing early Windows architecture. This is a great question about systems programming history.

Let me think through what I know about Windows 3.1's architecture:

1. **Windows 3.1 as a DOS application**: Yes, Windows 3.1 was launched from DOS (WIN.COM). But once it took control of the hardware, it largely bypassed DOS for most operations. It used DOS for file I/O initially but had its own memory manager, GDI, USER, KERNEL modules.

2. **Multitasking model**: Windows 3.1 did NOT have true preemptive multitasking. It used cooperative multitasking (also called "cooperative scheduling"). The KERNEL module (KERNEL.EXE) managed task switching. Each task (application) would run until it voluntarily yielded control back to the KERNEL via system calls or message processing.

3. **How it worked under DOS**: 
   - Windows 3.1 loaded itself into memory (typically in extended/expanded memory)
   - It set up its own GDT (Global Descriptor Table) for protected mode (286/386)
   - On 386 Enhanced mode, Windows used virtual 8086 mode to run DOS applications in a sandbox while the Windows kernel ran in protected mode
   - The KERNEL managed memory segments, handles, and the message queue
   - Applications communicated via messages (WM_PAINT, WM_TIMER, etc.) and the cooperative scheduler would switch between them
   - The KERNEL loaded each application's code into memory segments and managed switching between them

4. **The multitasking mechanism**:
   - Cooperative multitasking: The KERNEL.EXE maintained a list of running tasks
   - When a task made a system call (like GetMsg, PeekMessage, or any USER/GDI call), control would return to KERNEL
   - KERNEL would then check if another task had pending messages or needed CPU time
   - If so, it would switch to that task (change segment registers, stack pointers)
   - If no task needed service, it would return to the current task
   - This is why poorly-written applications could hang Windows 3.1 - they never yielded back to KERNEL

5

I have thought about this long enough; time to give my answer.
html:
How Windows 3.1 Achieved Multitasking on a Non-Multitasking DOS Host

Windows 3.1's multitasking was cooperative, not preemptive. The trick was that Windows 3.1, once launched, essentially took over the CPU from DOS and implemented its own scheduler, memory manager, and virtual-8086 sandbox in protected mode. DOS became a vestigial bootloader, not the runtime OS.

Key Insight

Windows 3.1 was a DOS application only at the moment of launch. Once WIN.COM finished loading the Windows kernel into protected-mode memory, DOS was effectively parked. Windows 3.1 operated as a 16-bit protected-mode OS with its own scheduler, GDT, and segment management.

The Architecture Stack

1

DOS Boot & Handoff

User types WIN at the DOS prompt. WIN.COM (a tiny real-mode loader) reads KERNEL.EXE, USER.EXE, GDI.EXE, and SYSTEM.INI from disk. It sets up the Global Descriptor Table (GDT), switches the CPU to protected mode (80286+) or Virtual 8086 mode (80386+), then transfers control to KERNEL.EXE. From this point, DOS is no longer in control.

2

KERNEL.EXE — The Microkernel & Scheduler

KERNEL.EXE is the heart of the system. It owns the CPU dispatch loop, manages the handle table (a flat array of 4-byte slots mapping handles → segment:offset), loads/unloads application code segments, and implements the cooperative task switcher. There is no timer interrupt driving context switches — switching happens only at well-defined yield points.

3

USER.EXE & GDI.EXE — The API Layers

USER.EXE manages windows, messages, menus, and the message queue. GDI.EXE handles drawing, fonts, and device contexts. Both are loaded as resident DLLs (16-bit NE-format modules) mapped into the same address space. Applications call these APIs via the handle-based thunking layer.

4

Application Code — Native 16-bit Segments

Windows apps are compiled as New Executable (NE) files. The linker produces segmented 16-bit code with no runtime wrapper. KERNEL.EXE loads these segments into the 64K-granularity segment table and assigns each app its own task handle. The app runs as native machine code — no interpreter, no managed runtime.

Cooperative Multitasking: The Actual Mechanism

What "Cooperative" Means Here

  • The CPU runs one task at a time. There is no hardware timer interrupt forcing a switch.
  • A task voluntarily yields back to KERNEL whenever it calls a system function: GetMessage(), PeekMessage(), SendMessage(), DispatchMessage(), LoadLibrary(), GlobalAlloc(), SetTimer() processing, etc.
  • At each yield point, KERNEL inspects the message queue and the timer queue. If another task has pending messages or a timer has expired, KERNEL switches segment registers (CS, DS, SS) and the stack pointer to that task.
  • If no other task needs service, control returns to the same task and it continues executing.

Why This Worked (and Why It Broke)

  • It worked because 16-bit Windows apps were message-driven. The normal app loop was GetMessage → DispatchMessage → … → GetMessage. Each call to GetMessage was a yield point. A well-behaved app returned to KERNEL hundreds of times per second.
  • It broke when an app ran a long compute loop without calling any API. The task never yielded → the entire system froze. This was the infamous "Windows 3.1 hang" from a single misbehaving application.
  • Windows 3.1 also had time-slicing in its timer dispatch: if a task had been running for a fixed number of KERNEL cycles, KERNEL would preempt it at the next API call boundary, but it could never preempt mid-instruction.

Virtual 8086 Mode: Running DOS Apps Under Windows

386 Enhanced Mode (Win3.1's Killer Feature)

On an 80386+, Windows 3.1 ran in Virtual 8086 mode — the CPU's protected-mode feature that lets multiple independent real-mode "virtual machines" share one protected-mode OS.

  • Windows itself ran as the supervisor in ring 0, owning the GDT, IDT, and page tables.
  • Each DOS application ran in a Virtual 8086 task — a sandboxed real-mode VM with its own segment table and trap flags.
  • When a DOS app executed an INT 21h, INT 10h, or touched a protected-mode resource, a trap fired back to the Windows KERNEL, which emulated or virtualized the call.
  • Multiple DOS apps could run "simultaneously" because the CPU multiplexed their virtual 8086 tasks under Windows' cooperative scheduler.

Standard mode (286) had no virtual 8086 support — DOS apps ran in a single real-mode window, and true multitasking was limited to 16-bit Windows apps only.

Memory & Segment Management

ComponentRoleKey Detail
KERNEL.EXE Microkernel, scheduler, handle table, task manager Owns the 64K-segment GDT. Each loaded module (app or DLL) gets a segment descriptor. Task switch = load new CS/DS/SS from the GDT entry for the target task.
Handle Table Indirection layer for all objects (windows, bitmaps, timers, memory blocks) 4-byte entries: [segment:offset, flags, refcount, …]. Apps never hold raw pointers — they hold handles, which KERNEL can relocate or swap out of memory.
USER.EXE Window manager, message routing Maintains per-task message queues. GetMessage is the primary cooperative yield point.
GDI.EXE Graphics device interface Device contexts, fonts, bitmaps. Called via handles. Traps to KERNEL on resource allocation.
NE Loader Loads New Executables into segments Resolves import tables, fixes segment:offset pointers, assigns task handles. No relocation beyond segment base.

What Happened at a Task Switch (Low-Level)

A simplified sequence when KERNEL switches from Task A to Task B:

  1. Task A calls GetMessage() → traps to KERNEL (via INT 21h or a far call through a fixed GDT descriptor).
  2. KERNEL checks Task A's message queue — empty. Checks global timer queue — a timer is due for Task B.
  3. KERNEL saves Task A's IP, SP, CS, DS, SS into its task control block (TCB).
  4. KERNEL loads Task B's saved CS, DS, SS from the GDT (these are 16-bit segment selectors pointing to the app's code/data/stack descriptors).
  5. KERNEL jumps to Task B's saved IP. Task B resumes executing as if it never stopped.
  6. When Task B finishes its message processing and calls GetMessage again, KERNEL may switch back to Task A or to Task C.

Crucially: there is no page-level isolation between tasks. All 16-bit Windows apps share the same 1 MB address space. A buggy pointer in App A can corrupt App B's memory. Windows 3.1's "protection" is purely cooperative discipline, not hardware enforcement.

Historical Technical Documents & References

Primary Sources (Still Findable)

  • Programmer's Guide to Microsoft Windows 3.1 (Microsoft Press, 1992) — describes the KERNEL/USER/GDI API surface, handle model, and NE loading.
  • Microsoft Windows 3.1 DDK documentation — the WINEXES.TXT and KERNEL.TXT reference files describe internal KERNEL functions like GetTaskHandle, SetTaskHandle, GlobalLock, GlobalUnlock, and the task-switch loop. These are available in archived DDK CD-ROMs.
  • Raymond Chen's The Old New Thing blog — extensive posts on Windows 3.1 internals, handle tables, cooperative multitasking, and the NE loader. Search for "Win3.1" or "cooperative multitasking."
  • Undocumented Windows 3.1 Secrets by Jeffrey Richter (Microsoft Systems Journal, 1993) — reverse-engineered KERNEL internals, task switching, and the message queue implementation.
  • Windows Internals by Matt Pietrek (Addison-Wesley, 1993) — chapter-by-chapter dissection of KERNEL.EXE, USER.EXE, GDI.EXE, the NE format, and the 386 Enhanced mode virtual 8086 machinery. This is arguably the definitive book on Win3.1 architecture.
  • Intel 80386 Programmer's Reference Manual — the Virtual 8086 mode, GDT, IDT, and task-switch mechanics that Windows 3.1 built on.
  • Microsoft Windows Programming Guide (1990, Win 3.0 era) — earlier, but describes the cooperative model and the KERNEL's role before 386 Enhanced mode existed.

Many of these are available on the Internet Archive (archive.org) as scanned PDFs. The Matt Pietrek book in particular has been scanned and is freely accessible.

Common Misconception

"Windows ran on top of DOS" is misleading shorthand. More precisely: Windows used DOS as a bootloader and initial file-I/O layer. Once in protected mode, Windows had its own memory manager (no INT 21h for heap allocation), its own scheduler, and its own display subsystem. DOS was trapped (in 386 Enhanced mode) or parked (in Standard mode). Calling Windows a "DOS application" is like calling a rocket a "truck" because it was launched from a truck bed.

Quick Comparison: Win 3.1 vs. Modern Preemptive Models

AspectWindows 3.1 (Cooperative)Windows 95+ / Modern (Preemptive)

instruction:
I'm working on 2 different branches: release and development. 
I noticed I still need to integrate some changes that were committed to the release branch back into the development branch.  
The problem is I don't need all of the commit, only some hunks in certain files, so a simple  
```git cherry-pick bc66559
```
does not do the trick.  
When I do a
```git show bc66559
```
I can see the diff but don't really know a good way of applying that partially to my current working tree.
cot:
The user wants to apply only specific hunks from a commit (bc66559) from their release branch to their development branch. They can see the diff with `git show bc66559` but don't know how to apply it partially.

Let me think about the best approaches:

1. **`git show bc66559 | git apply --recount`** - Apply the full patch, but this applies everything. Not quite what they want.

2. **`git show bc66559 > patch.diff` then manually edit the patch file** - Remove unwanted hunks, then apply with `git apply patch.diff`. This is a classic approach.

3. **`git show bc66559 | git apply`** with selective editing.

4. **Using `git diff` with specific file paths** - `git show bc66559 -- path/to/file1 path/to/file2` to limit to certain files, then apply.

5. **Interactive approach**: Generate the patch, edit it to remove unwanted hunks, then apply.

6. **`git cherry-pick --no-commit`** then selectively stage/unstage hunks with `git add -p` - This is probably the most elegant modern approach. You cherry-pick without committing, then use `git add -p` to selectively stage only the hunks you want, then commit.

7. **`git show bc66559` piped to a patch file, edit, then `git apply`**.

8. **Using `git diff bc66559^ bc66559 -- file1 file2`** to get diffs for specific files only.

Let me structure this as a comprehensive guide with multiple approaches, from simplest to most flexible.

The most practical approaches:
- **Approach 1**: `git cherry-pick --no-commit` + `git add -p` (most elegant, interactive)
- **Approach 2**: Generate patch file, edit it, apply it (more control over exact hunks)
- **Approach 3**: `git show` limited to specific files, then apply (file-level granularity)

Let me present these clearly with code examples.
html:
Applying a Commit Partially: Selective Hunk Integration

You have three solid strategies depending on how granular you need to be. The cherry-pick + interactive add combo is the most ergonomic for hunk-level selection; the patch-file edit approach gives you surgical control; the file-scoped diff is fastest when you just need whole files.

Approach 1 — Cherry-pick without committing, then select hunks interactively

This is the most Git-native workflow. You land the commit's changes in your working tree, then pick exactly which hunks to keep before committing.

bash
# On your development branch
git checkout development

# Apply the commit's changes to working tree WITHOUT committing
git cherry-pick --no-commit bc66559

html:
Cultural Victory in Civilization V: The City Count Dilemma

The commonly cited "sweet spot" is 6–8 cities for a cultural victory in Civ V: Brave New World. This number isn't a hard rule—it's an emergent optimum born from the tension between fixed policy costs, per-city culture scaling, and the opportunity cost of expansion.

Understanding the "Plateau" Mechanic

What's Actually Fixed vs. Variable

The total culture cost for 36 social policies is fixed—it does not change based on how many cities you own. What changes is your culture generation rate and the opportunity cost of each additional city.

The "plateau" you're describing is really a diminishing-returns curve:

  • Early cities (1–4): Each new city dramatically boosts culture because you go from 1–2 generators to 3–4. Each city also gets a free culture-building slot (Monument, then Theater Square, etc.).
  • Mid cities (5–8): Culture per new city is lower because your existing cities already have buildings, and each new city starts at zero. However, you gain more total culture output.
  • Late cities (9+): Marginal culture gain per city shrinks. You also face happiness penalties (−1 per city beyond your happiness cap), which suppress culture-generating buildings and slow growth, effectively reducing your culture per city.

City 1–4

High ROI

Each city roughly doubles or adds ~50% to total culture output. Monuments, libraries, and early wonders hit every city. The culture-per-turn jump is dramatic.

City 5–8

Diminishing but strong

Each new city adds meaningful but smaller culture. You're still gaining more than you're spending on maintenance. This is where the optimal range lives.

City 9+

Plateau / Negative

Happiness penalties kick in. Unhappy cities stop growing, which caps their culture output. Maintenance costs rise. You're spreading your gold and production thinner without a proportional culture return.

Why 6–8 Is the Sweet Spot

Factor Fewer Cities (3–5) Optimal (6–8) Many Cities (10+)
Total Culture/Turn Low. Vulnerable to a single city being raided or falling. Strong and resilient. Multiple generators keep pace even if one lags. High gross output, but each city is smaller and less productive.
City Culture per City High per city (large pop, many buildings). Good balance of size and count. Low per city—small, unhappiness-limited populations.
Gold & Production Strain Minimal. Easy to maintain. Manageable with good trade routes and commerce policies. Severe. Maintenance + units + buildings eat your gold.
Happiness Pressure Low. Moderate—manageable with happiness buildings, policies, and trade. High. Unhappiness caps growth, capping culture.
Vulnerability to Aggression High—losing 1 of 4 cities is devastating. Resilient—losing 1 of 7 is painful but survivable. Spread thin. Many targets, each individually weak.
Wonder Competition Hard to rush Wonders with few cities. Sufficient production pool to contest key Wonders. Production diluted across many small cities.
Key Insight: Culture Scales with Population, Not City Count

Each city's culture output is roughly proportional to its population (plus buildings). A city of size 12 generates far more culture than two cities of size 6. Spreading 120 citizens across 10 tiny cities produces less culture than concentrating them in 6–7 large cities. This is the core reason the curve plateaus.

Does the Ideal Number Change Over Time?

1

Early Game (Ancient → Classical)

Target: 4–5 cities. You need breadth for survival, early wonders (Great Wall, Oracle), and the first 2–3 policy tiers. Each new city is a huge culture multiplier here. Don't over-expand; you need production for defense.

2

Mid Game (Medieval → Renaissance)

Target: 6–7 cities. This is where the culture engine really kicks in. You're unlocking the Tradition → Aesthetics → Freedom path. Each city should be growing toward size 10–15. Trade routes are now generating significant culture (with Commerce). This is the critical window for the 36-policy grind.

3

Late Game (Industrial → Modern)

Hold at 7–8; resist the urge to expand further. Your last few policies (the most expensive ones) cost 250–400+ culture each. You want your existing cities maximized—large populations, all culture buildings, Great People, and Wonders. A new city at this point adds almost nothing to your culture curve while stealing gold and production.

4

Endgame (Final Policies + Wonder)

Stop expanding entirely. Your last 3–5 policies and the required Wonder are the bottleneck. Pour all resources into your best 4–5 cities. Every turn spent building a Settler is a turn not building the final Wonder.

The Policy Cost Curve (Why the Plateau Feels Real)

Approximate Culture Costs Across the 36-Policy Path

The cheapest policies (Tradition tier 1) cost 0–36 culture. The most expensive (Freedom tier 5, Order tier 5) can cost 250–400+ culture each. This means:

  • Policies 1–12 (early tiers): Cheap. You'll hit these quickly even with 3–4 cities. The "plateau" feels nonexistent here.
  • Policies 13–24 (mid tiers): Moderate cost. Your culture engine needs 6+ cities to keep the pace without stalling. This is where expansion still pays off.
  • Policies 25–36 (late tiers): Expensive. Each policy can take 10–20 turns of pure culture accumulation. Adding a 9th city at this point adds ~2–4 culture/turn—barely moves the needle. You're better off growing existing cities.
The Hidden Trap: Over-Expansion Kills Cultural Victories

Players who expand to 12–15 cities often never reach 36 policies. The happiness cap prevents city growth, culture buildings become unaffordable, and the AI's culture race (especially on higher difficulties where AI gets culture bonuses) overtakes you. More cities ≠ faster culture victory. Often the opposite.

Practical City-Count Guidelines by Difficulty

Difficulty Recommended Cities Rationale
Settler → Chieftain 5–6 AI is weak; you can afford a smaller, more focused empire. Culture victory is relatively easy.
Warlord → Prince 6–8 AI gets culture bonuses. You need enough cities to keep pace but not so many you drown in maintenance.
King → Emperor 7–9 AI is aggressive and culture-competitive. Slightly more cities help, but you must invest heavily in happiness and culture buildings.
Deity 8–10 AI has massive culture bonuses. You genuinely need more generators, but each city must be optimized (Monument + Library + Theater Square + Great People + Wonders).
Actionable Rule of Thumb

Build cities until your culture-per-turn stops increasing meaningfully, then stop. Concretely: if adding a new city increases your total culture/turn by less than 15–20%, you've passed the inflection point. At that stage, invest in growing existing cities, building culture wonders, and acquiring Great People instead.

Maximizing Culture Per City (What Makes Each City Count)

Build Priority Per City

  1. Monument — immediate culture boost
  2. Library — science + culture
  3. Theater Square — large flat culture bonus
  4. Amphitheater — culture multiplier on Theater Square
  5. Opera House (BNW) — culture + happiness
  6. Music School (BNW) — culture + happiness

Empire-Level Multipliers

  • Policy Tradition → Piety → Aesthetics → Freedom → Order path
  • Wonders Great Library, Chichen Itza, Forbidden Palace, Taj Mahal, Big Ben, Sistine Chapel
  • Great People Great Artists/Composers/Writers (one-time culture bursts)
  • Trade Routes Internal routes with Commerce give culture
  • City-State Allies Cultural city-states provide passive culture

Bottom Line

The ideal city count is not a fixed number—it's a dynamic target that shifts from ~4 in the Ancient Era to ~7–8 in the Industrial Era, then freezes. The cultural victory race is fundamentally a quality-over-quantity problem: a handful of well-developed, happy, culture-optimized cities will outpace a sprawling, unhappy, spread-thin empire every time.

The "plateau" is real, but it's not a culture-cost wall—it's a diminishing-returns wall on your culture generation side. Recognize it early, stop expanding, and pour everything into your existing engine.

How to find if a customer is logged in or not in Magento 2.
If the customer is logged in then how to get customer data from a session?
cot:
The user is asking about Magento 2 development - specifically:
1. How to check if a customer is logged in
2. How to get customer data from the session if they are logged in

This is a technical development question about Magento 2's customer session/authentication system. Let me provide a comprehensive, well-structured answer covering:

- The primary way to check login status (CustomerSession model)
- Getting customer data from the session
- Alternative approaches (Context, helper classes)
- Code examples for different contexts (controller, model, block/template)
- Key methods and their return values

Let me structure this with cards, code boxes, tables, and callouts for maximum clarity.
html:
Detecting Customer Login & Retrieving Session Data in Magento 2

In Magento 2, customer authentication state is managed through the \Magento\Customer\Model\Session class. You can check login status via isLoggedIn() and pull the full customer object via getCustomer(). This session model is injectable anywhere via DI — controllers, blocks, helpers, and models.

⚡ Quick Answer

Check login: $session->isLoggedIn() → returns true or false
Get customer data: $session->getCustomer() → returns a \Magento\Customer\Api\Data\CustomerInterface object

1 — Check if a Customer Is Logged In

The canonical method is isLoggedIn() on the Customer\Model\Session. Under the hood it checks whether a customer ID exists in the PHP session under customer_id.

PHP — Controller / Model / Block (via DI)
<?php
namespace Vendor\Module\...;

use Magento\Customer\Model\Session as CustomerSession;

class SomeController extends \Magento\Framework\App\Action\Action

No one at our local bookstore could offer any advice. Is there a kid-friendly imprint or other resource I could use to help her find something appropriate? My preference is for physical books but I'm willing to explore digital options.

Yes — manga absolutely has a strong kid-friendly ecosystem. There are dedicated imprints, curated lists, and well-known series made specifically for readers aged 6–12. Below is a practical guide to finding age-appropriate manga in both physical and digital formats.

1. Dedicated Kid-Friendly Manga Imprints

U.S. Publishers

  • VIZ Kids / VIZ Media Kids — The single most important imprint to look for. VIZ publishes a curated line of manga explicitly aimed at readers 8–12. Look for the small "Kids" logo on the spine. Titles like Yotsuba&!, My Little Monster (Komi Can't Communicate) early volumes, and Chi's Sweet Home fall here.
  • Kodansha USA – Jump line (select titles) — Some Shōnen Jump titles are age-appropriate for 9-year-olds (see table below). Look for the "Rated T" or "Rated T+" content advisory on the back cover.
  • Seven Seas Entertainment – Ghost Ship & general line — Publishes several all-ages and gentle slice-of-life manga (e.g., My Neighbor Seki early arcs).
  • Bluewater / Yen Press — Occasionally carries all-ages titles; less curated for kids but worth browsing.

Japanese Imprint Context

Understanding the Japanese magazines helps you filter at the bookstore:

  • Kodomo Shōnen manga — Literally "children's boys' manga," but girls read them too. These are the safest starting point. Examples: Doraemon, Chi's Sweet Home.
  • Shōjo (girls') manga — Aimed at ages 12–18. Some early arcs of popular shōjo are fine for a 9-year-old, but many contain romantic content. Use the content advisories.
  • Shōnen (boys') manga — Ages 12+. Many are too mature for 9. Stick to the lighter action/comedy titles noted below.
  • Seinen / Josei — Adult. Avoid.
🛍️ Bookstore Tip

Ask staff to pull the VIZ Kids shelf specifically. Many bookstores shelve all manga together in one large section, which is why a clerk without manga knowledge may not know which titles are kid-appropriate. If you see a content advisory box on the back cover (e.g., "Rated T" = teens 13+, "Rated T+" = mild), titles without that box or rated "All Ages" are your safest bet.

2. Starter Series for a 9-Year-Old

Series Genre / Tone Why It Works at 9 Format
Chi's Sweet Home VIZ Kids Slice-of-life / Comedy A kitten's daily adventures. Gentle, funny, zero conflict or violence. Great for reluctant readers. Print (12 vols) · Manga Plus (free digital)
Yotsuba&! VIZ Kids Slice-of-life / Comedy A curious 5-year-old explores everyday life. Warm, wholesome, hilarious. Often the #1 recommendation for new manga readers of any age. Print (15 vols) · Available on many library apps
Doraemon VIZ Kids Sci-fi / Comedy Classic Japanese series about a robot cat and a boy. Episodic, low-stakes, endlessly charming. Print (many vols) · Digital via VIZ app
My Neighbor Seki All Ages School comedy A quiet kid tries to stay invisible in class; his seatmate is a prankster. Very gentle, funny, short chapters. Print (14 vols) · Digital
Pokémon Adventures All Ages Adventure / Fantasy Follows the Pokémon game storyline in manga form. A natural bridge if she already knows Pokémon. Print (many vols) · Digital
Cardcaptor Sakura Rated T Magic / Adventure A girl collects magical cards. Light romance in later volumes, but early arcs are very age-appropriate. A classic for girls discovering manga. Print (12 vols) · Digital
Spy × Family (early arcs) Rated T+ Comedy / Spy The daughter character (Anya) is a kid, and early chapters are comedy-driven. Parent-preview first — some action and mild romance later on. Print · VIZ app / Shonen Jump digital
My Hero Academia (vols 1–4) Rated T+ Superhero / Action Very popular with tweens. Early volumes are school-focused with mild action. Check with her whether she can handle occasional cartoonish violence. Print · VIZ app / Shonen Jump digital
⚠️ A Note on "Rated T+" Titles

Series like My Hero Academia and Spy × Family are enormously popular with 9-year-olds, but they carry a T+ advisory (mild violence, occasional suggestive humor). They are not "kid-only" titles. If you want a completely safe first purchase, start with the VIZ Kids titles above, then graduate to T+ series once she's comfortable.

3. Where to Find & Browse (Physical + Digital)

1

Use the VIZ Kids Catalog as Your Master List

Go to viz.com/kids. Every title on that page is vetted for ages 8–12. You can filter by genre, browse covers, and read free sample chapters. This single page eliminates 80% of the guesswork.

2

Check MangaPlus by SHUEISHA (Free Digital)

mangaplus.shueisha.co.jp streams dozens of series legally for free. Look for titles tagged "All Ages" or under the VIZ Kids filter. Great for letting her sample before you buy a physical volume. Available on iOS, Android, and web.

3

Use Your Local Library (Often Overlooked)

Most public libraries carry manga, often shelved under J821 or in a graphic-novel section. Ask a librarian to pull the Yotsuba&! or Chi's Sweet Home series. Many libraries also offer Libby / OverDrive digital manga borrowing — free, no bookstore trip needed.

4

Online Physical Purchase with Age Filtering

Amazon: search "manga ages 8-12" or filter by publisher "VIZ Kids." RightStuf / Books-A-Million / Barnes & Noble all carry VIZ Kids shelf sections. Crunchyroll Store also stocks physical manga and has age-appropriate collections.

5

Consult Curated Community Lists

The subreddit r/manga and r/childrensmanga have recurring "best manga for kids" threads. The Goodreads list "Manga for Kids" is community-vetted. For a Japanese-language perspective, the National Diet Library of Japan publishes age-rated manga recommendations (translated summaries available).

4. A Practical "First Purchase" Plan

🎁 Volume 1 Gift

Yotsuba&! Vol. 1 — Buy one physical copy. It's the safest, funniest, most universally loved entry point. If she laughs, you've confirmed she likes the medium.

All Ages

📱 Free Sampling

Install MangaPlus on her tablet or your phone. Let her browse Chi's Sweet Home or Doraemon chapters for free before you commit to a print purchase.

Free

📚 Library Visit

Bring her to the graphic-novel / manga section and let her pick a cover that looks fun. Nine-year-olds are great at choosing based on art style. A librarian can help if she gravitates toward something with a T+ rating.

Free

5. Key Specs at a Glance

VIZ Kids Line 50+ titles Ages 8–12, vetted by VIZ editors
MangaPlus (Free) 300+ series Shueisha's official legal reader
Typical Manga Volume ~200 pages Right-to-left reading; B6 or A5 trim
Avg. Price (Print) $12–$16 Paperback per volume; hardcover ~$25
✅ Bottom Line

Start at viz.com/kids, buy one physical copy of Yotsuba&! or Chi's Sweet Home, and let her browse MangaPlus for free to find her own favorites. The VIZ Kids imprint is the single most reliable "kid-safe" manga filter in English-language publishing, and it exists specifically because parents asked for it. You don't need a manga-savvy bookstore clerk — the imprint does the vetting for you.

I'm looking for a precise piece of information in a database which I have no knowledge about. The database is on a separate machine, but I can log into it, and launch a ```psql``` command line, with administrator rights.
It's a third-party product, and they are slow to answer questions. I know the data is inside that database, so I want to do a little bit of reverse-engineering.
Given a table name, is it possible to get a list of the names of the columns in that table?
For example, in SQL Server, it's possible to dump a table into a reusable ```CREATE``` statement, which textually lists all the columns the table is composed of.
cot:
The user is asking about PostgreSQL (they mention `psql` command line) and want to know how to get a list of column names for a given table. They want to reverse-engineer a third-party product's database. They mention SQL Server's ability to dump a CREATE statement as context for what they're used to.

Let me provide a comprehensive answer covering multiple approaches in PostgreSQL to get column information for a table, since they have admin access and psql available. I'll cover:

1. `\d` meta-command in psql
2. `information_schema.columns` query
3. `pg_catalog.pg_attribute` query
4. `\d+` for more detail
5. Generating a CREATE TABLE statement equivalent (like SQL Server's scripting)
6. Maybe a quick way to get just column names

Let me structure this clearly with cards, code boxes, and tables.
html:
Yes — trivially. PostgreSQL exposes full table metadata through both psql meta-commands and standard catalog queries. You can get column names in one keystroke, or reconstruct a full CREATE TABLE statement equivalent to what you'd get from SQL Server's "Script Table As" feature.

Quickest Path: psql Meta-Command

Once you're inside the psql prompt, the \d family of backslash commands is the fastest way to inspect any table:

psql
\d schema_name.table_name

This prints the column list, data types, nullability, defaults, indexes, constraints, and more — all in one shot.

\d table

Columns, types, modifiers, indexes, constraints. The default view.

\d+ table

Everything \d shows plus storage stats, comments on columns, and visibility info.

\dt

List all tables in the current schema (useful for discovery when you don't yet know the table name).

SQL-Based Approaches (Scriptable & Copy-Paste Friendly)

1. information_schema.columns — ANSI Standard

Best for portability and readability. Returns one row per column:

SQL
SELECT column_name, data_type, is_nullable, column_default
FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_schema = 'public'
  AND table_name   = 'your_table'
ORDER BY ordinal_position;

2. pg_catalog.pg_attribute — Full Internal Detail

Exposes everything the engine knows: internal OIDs, storage parameters, generation expressions, etc. Use this when information_schema doesn't cover a feature (e.g., generated columns in PG 12+):

SQL
SELECT a.attname        AS column_name,
       format_type(a.atttypid, a.atttypmod) AS data_type,
       a.attnotnull     AS not_null,
       pg_get_expr(d.adbin, d.adrelid) AS default_expr
FROM pg_attribute a
LEFT JOIN pg_attrdef d ON d.adrelid = a.attrelid AND d.adnum = a.attnum
WHERE a.attrelid = 'public.your_table'::regclass
  AND a.attnum > 0
  AND NOT a.attisdropped
ORDER BY a.attnum;

Recreate the Full CREATE TABLE (SQL Server Equivalent)

Tip for reverse-engineering

SQL Server's "Script Table As → CREATE" has no single built-in equivalent in vanilla PostgreSQL, but you can reconstruct it in seconds with a one-liner using pg_dump or a catalog query.

Option A — pg_dump (single table)

bash
pg_dump -t "schema_name.table_name" --no-schema --no-data \
  -h remote_host -U admin_user dbname

Outputs the exact CREATE TABLE, CREATE INDEX, ALTER TABLE ADD CONSTRAINT statements — textually identical to what you'd get from SQL Server Management Studio.

Option B — In-Session Catalog Reconstruction

SQL
-- Columns only (compact, pipe-separated)
SELECT string_agg(
         attname || ' ' || format_type(atttypid, atttypmod),
         ', '
         ORDER BY attnum)
FROM pg_attribute
WHERE attrelid = 'public.your_table'::regclass
  AND attnum > 0
  AND NOT attisdropped;

Returns a single string like id integer, name text, created_at timestamp, status varchar(20) — easy to paste into a CREATE TABLE skeleton.

Discovery Helpers (When You Don't Know the Table Name Yet)

GoalCommandNotes
List all tables \dt or \dt+ * + adds size & description.
Search column names across all tables \d *pattern* psql glob; e.g. \d *customer*
Fuzzy search in catalog SQL ILIKE on information_schema.columns Useful for vendor tables with cryptic names.
View table row count / size \dt+ your_table Shows disk size, helps confirm you found the right table.
See foreign keys / relationships \d+ your_table Bottom section lists FKs, referenced tables.

Practical Workflow (Stepper)

1

Connect with admin privileges

psql -h <host> -U <admin_user> -d <dbname> — you already have this.

2

Identify the schema & table

Run \dn to list schemas, then \dt or \dt+ * to enumerate tables. Vendor products often hide data in a named schema like app, vendor, or a GUID-based name.

3

Dump the structure

\d+ target_table for a readable view, or pg_dump -t target_table --no-data for a copy-pasteable CREATE TABLE.

4

Spot the data

Once you know the columns, run SELECT * FROM target_table LIMIT 20; to confirm the table actually holds the information you need.

Caution with third-party vendor databases

Some products encrypt specific columns (via pgcrypto extensions) or store blobs. If you see columns typed as bytea or a vendor-specific encrypted type, the raw SELECT will return ciphertext. Check \dx inside psql to see which extensions are loaded — that's often the key to understanding what's encrypted and what isn't.

Bottom line

With \d+ table_name you get the column list in under two seconds. With pg_dump -t table_name --no-data you get the full CREATE TABLE script equivalent to SQL Server's scripting feature. No third-party vendor ticket needed.

I am using Visual Studio Code and have a fairly common project structure:
```├── client/
│   ├── tsconfig.json
├── shared/
├── server/
│   ├── tsconfig.json
├── project.json
```
The two tsconfig files have different settings (e.g. the one under ```client/``` targets ES5, the one under ```server/``` targets ES6). Note that there is no tsconfig in the root directory.
The problem is that I want the shared directory to be included in both projects. I can't do this using tsconfig because the ```exclude``` option won't let me include a folder that is in a higher directory than the tsconfig.json, and using ```files``` I have to constantly keep the list of files up to date as it doesn't support globs.
Note that I can compile fine by adding the shared folder into tsc, what I want is for the Visual Studio Code IDE to recognise the shared code for intellisense etc.
Is the only option to wait for filesGlob?
cot:
The user is asking about a TypeScript project structure in VS Code where they have a monorepo-like setup with client/, shared/, and server/ directories, each with their own tsconfig.json. The shared/ directory needs to be part of both projects, but they're having issues with IntelliSense in VS Code because:

1. `exclude` can't exclude a parent directory
2. `files` doesn't support globs
3. They want VS Code to recognize shared code for IntelliSense

Let me think about the solutions:

1. **`include` with relative paths** - Actually, TypeScript's `include` DOES support globs and CAN reference files outside the tsconfig directory using relative paths like `../shared/**/*.ts`. This is the key solution.

2. **Project References** - TypeScript's project references feature can handle this elegantly. You define shared as its own project and reference it from both client and server.

3. **Path mapping** - Using `paths` in tsconfig to map imports.

4. **Root tsconfig.json** - Creating a root tsconfig that includes shared.

5. **VS Code specific settings** - The `typescript.tsconfig` or workspace settings.

6. **The `include` option actually works** - This is the most direct answer. `include` supports globs and relative paths going up directories. The user seems to think it doesn't work, but it does.

7. **Project References** - This is the modern, best-practice approach for monorepos.

Let me structure a comprehensive answer covering:
- The direct fix (include with globs and relative paths)
- Project References (the proper monorepo solution)
- VS Code specific tips
- Why their assumptions about exclude/files are partially wrong

The key insight the user might be missing: `include` in tsconfig DOES support globs and DOES allow paths outside the current directory (using `../`). The `exclude` limitation they mention is real but irrelevant if you use `include` properly.

Let me write a thorough, practical response.
html:
Solving Shared Code IntelliSense in a Multi-tsconfig VS Code Project

You don't need to wait for filesGlob. TypeScript's include supports globs and paths outside the tsconfig directory (via ../). Combine that with Project References and you get full IntelliSense for shared/ in both projects.

Key Misconception

include does accept glob patterns and relative paths that traverse upward (e.g. "../shared/**/*.ts"). The exclude limitation you hit is real, but it's irrelevant once you use include correctly. You do not need files or a root tsconfig.

Option 1 — The Quick Fix: include with Globs

Each tsconfig.json simply adds shared/ via a glob in include:

client/tsconfig.json

JSON
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES5",
    "module": "commonjs",
    "outDir": "./dist",
    "rootDir": "..",          // ← critical
    "strict": true,
    "baseUrl": ".",
    "paths": {
      "shared/*": ["../shared/*"]
    }
  },
  "include": [
    "./src/**/*.ts",
    "../shared/**/*.ts"       // ← glob, parent dir, works!
  ],
  "exclude": ["node_modules", "dist"]
}

server/tsconfig.json

JSON
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES6",
    "module": "commonjs",
    "outDir": "./dist",
    "rootDir": "..",
    "strict": true,
    "baseUrl": ".",
    "paths": {
      "shared/*": ["../shared/*"]
    }
  },
  "include": [
    "./src/**/*.ts",
    "../shared/**/*.ts"       // ← same pattern
  ],
  "exclude": ["node_modules", "dist"]
}
⚠ rootDir Must Be Set

Because include now reaches outside the tsconfig folder, TypeScript needs "rootDir": ".." (the project root) to compute correct output paths. Without it, tsc will emit into dist/../shared/… and complain. The paths mapping lets you write import { X } from "shared/models" instead of import { X } from "../shared/models".

Option 2 — The Proper Solution: Project References

For a real monorepo, TypeScript Project References (TS 3.0+) is the recommended pattern. You make shared/ its own compilable project and both client and server reference it.

1

Create shared/tsconfig.json

JSON
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES5",          // lowest common target
    "module": "commonjs",
    "declaration": true,       // emit .d.ts for consumers
    "outDir": "./dist",
    "composite": true,         // ← required for project refs
    "strict": true
  },
  "include": ["./**/*.ts"]
}
2

Add references in client & server tsconfigs

client/tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES5",
    "module": "commonjs",
    "outDir": "./dist",
    "strict": true
  },
  "include": ["./src/**/*.ts"],
  "references": [
    { "path": "../shared" }   // ← VS Code IntelliSense follows this
  ]
}
server/tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES6",
    "module": "commonjs",
    "outDir": "./dist",
    "strict": true
  },
  "include": ["./src/**/*.ts"],
  "references": [
    { "path": "../shared" }
  ]
}
3

Add a root tsconfig.json (optional but recommended)

tsconfig.json (root)
{
  "files": [],
  "references": [
    { "path": "./shared" },
    { "path": "./client" },
    { "path": "./server" }
  ]
}

Run tsc -b at the root to build everything in dependency order. VS Code auto-detects this file and wires up IntelliSense across all three projects.

Why Project References Win
  • VS Code IntelliSense follows references automatically — no glob hacks needed.
  • declaration: true in shared/ means client/server read .d.ts files instead of re-compiling the source.
  • Each project keeps its own target, module, lib settings cleanly separated.
  • Incremental builds: tsc -b only rebuilds what changed.

Option 3 — VS Code–Only Workarounds

If you can't restructure configs, these VS Code settings help IntelliSense "see" the shared folder:

SettingWhereWhat It Does
"typescript.tsconfig" .vscode/settings.json Points VS Code to a specific tsconfig to use for IntelliSense. Useful when VS Code picks the wrong one.
"typescript.tsserver.experimental.enableProjectDiagnostics" .vscode/settings.json Forces TS server to load all projects in the workspace, not just the one for the active file.
"editor.defaultFormatter" + "typescript.preferences.importModuleSpecifier" .vscode/settings.json Controls how auto-imports resolve paths across folders.
"files.exclude" / "search.exclude" .vscode/settings.json Not IntelliSense-related, but keeps the Explorer clean when shared/ appears in multiple projects.
.vscode/settings.json
{
  "typescript.tsserver.experimental.enableProjectDiagnostics": true,
  "typescript.preferences.importModuleSpecifier": "non-relative"
}

Why Your Original Assumptions Were Close but Not Quite Right

exclude limitation

True

You can't exclude a parent directory. But you almost never need to if you use include with explicit globs — include is opt-in, so anything not listed is implicitly excluded.

files has no globs

Half-true

files is indeed a literal list. But include (which you probably meant) does support ** globs and relative parent paths. The docs sometimes blur the two.

Wait for filesGlob?

No

It was never added as a separate option because include already does exactly that. The TS team closed the filesGlob issue (microsoft/TypeScript#2472) pointing to include.

Recommended Final Structure

Project Tree
project/
├── tsconfig.json              ← root "solution" tsconfig (references only)
├── shared/
│   ├── tsconfig.json          ← composite: true, declaration: true
│   └── models/
│       └── User.ts
├── client/
│   ├── tsconfig.json          ← references: [{ path: "../shared" }]
│   └── src/
│       └── App.ts             ← import { User } from "shared/models/User"
└── server/
    ├── tsconfig.json          ← references: [{ path: "../shared" }]
    └── src/
        └── api.ts             ← import { User } from "shared/models/User"
Build Command

tsc -b at the project root builds shared → client and shared → server in correct dependency order. Add it to your project.json scripts or a package.json script.

Run tsc -b at the root to build everything in dependency order. VS Code auto-detects this file and wires up IntelliSense across all three projects.

Why Project References Win
  • VS Code IntelliSense follows references automatically — no glob hacks needed.
  • declaration: true in shared/ means client/server read .d.ts files instead of re-compiling the source.
  • Each project keeps its own target, module, lib settings cleanly separated.
  • Incremental builds: tsc -b only rebuilds what changed.

Option 3 — VS Code–Only Workarounds

If you can't restructure configs, these VS Code settings help IntelliSense "see" the shared folder:

SettingWhereWhat It Does
"typescript.tsconfig" .vscode/settings.json Points VS Code to a specific tsconfig to use for IntelliSense. Useful when VS Code picks the wrong one.
"typescript.tsserver.experimental.enableProjectDiagnostics" .vscode/settings.json Forces TS server to load all projects in the workspace, not just the one for the active file.
"editor.defaultFormatter" + "typescript.preferences.importModuleSpecifier" .vscode/settings.json Controls how auto-imports resolve paths across folders.
"files.exclude" / "search.exclude" .vscode/settings.json Not IntelliSense-related, but keeps the Explorer clean when shared/ appears in multiple projects.
.vscode/settings.json
{
  "typescript.tsserver.experimental.enableProjectDiagnostics": true,
  "typescript.preferences.importModuleSpecifier": "non-relative"
}

Why Your Original Assumptions Were Close but Not Quite Right

exclude limitation

True

You can't exclude a parent directory. But you almost never need to if you use include with explicit globs — include is opt-in, so anything not listed is implicitly excluded.

files has no globs

Half-true

files is indeed a literal list. But include (which you probably meant) does support ** globs and relative parent paths. The docs sometimes blur the two.

Wait for filesGlob?

No

It was never added as a separate option because include already does exactly that. The TS team closed the filesGlob issue (microsoft/TypeScript#2472) pointing to include.

Recommended Final Structure

Project Tree
project/
├── tsconfig.json              ← root "solution" tsconfig (references only)
├── shared/
│   ├── tsconfig.json          ← composite: true, declaration: true
│   └── models/
│       └── User.ts
├── client/
│   ├── tsconfig.json          ← references: [{ path: "../shared" }]
│   └── src/
│       └── App.ts             ← import { User } from "shared/models/User"
└── server/
    ├── tsconfig.json          ← references: [{ path: "../shared" }]
    └── src/
        └── api.ts             ← import { User } from "shared/models/User"
Build Command

tsc -b at the project root builds shared → client and shared → server in correct dependency order. Add it to your project.json scripts or a package.json script.

The user has a C# extension method that serializes an object to XML and saves it to a file. They want to modify it so that instead of saving to a file, it returns the XML as a string.

Key issues with their current code:
1. The extension method syntax is wrong - `this T toSerialize` is not valid C# syntax. Extension methods need `this` before the type, and the class must be static. The generic constraint is also missing.
2. They're using `XmlSerializer` which requires knowing the type at construction time.
3. They need to change from `StreamWriter` (file output) to `StringWriter` (string output).

Let me provide a corrected, working version that returns a string. I'll also note the issues with their current code and provide a clean solution.

The fix is straightforward: replace `StreamWriter` with `StringWriter`, and return the string content. I should also fix the extension method syntax properly.
html:
Convert File Serialization → String Serialization

The fix is minimal: swap StreamWriter (file-backed) for StringWriter (memory-backed), and return the resulting string. However, your current extension method also has a syntax issue that needs correcting.

⚠️ Syntax Issue in Your Current Code

this T toSerialize is not valid C#. In an extension method, this goes before the type, and the containing class must be static. Generic constraints are also required for XmlSerializer to compile.

Corrected Extension Method (Returns XML String)

C#
public static class XmlExtensions
{
    public static string SerializeObject<T>(this T toSerialize, string filename = null)
    {
        var xmlSerializer = new XmlSerializer(typeof(T));

        using var stringWriter = new StringWriter();
        xmlSerializer.Serialize(stringWriter, toSerialize);

        string xml = stringWriter.ToString();

        // Optional: still save to file if a filename is provided
        if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(filename))
        {
            File.WriteAllText(filename, xml);
        }

        return xml;
    }
}

Usage

C#
var myObj = new MySettings { Name = "Alice", Level = 42 };

// Get XML as a string
string xmlString = myObj.SerializeObject();

// Optionally also write to disk
string xmlString = myObj.SerializeObject("settings.xml");

What Changed & Why

AspectOriginal (File)Fixed (String)
Writer new StreamWriter(filename) new StringWriter()
Output Written to disk Returned via stringWriter.ToString()
Resource cleanup Manual .Close() using var (auto-disposes)
Generic syntax this T toSerialize ❌ SerializeObject<T>(this T …) ✅
Containing class Not shown Must be public static class

Key Points to Remember

🔒 XmlSerializer Needs a Concrete Type

new XmlSerializer(typeof(T)) works because the compiler resolves T at the call site. If you pass a base type and expect a derived runtime type, you'll get a serialization error. Use toSerialize.GetType() instead if you need runtime-type fidelity:

new XmlSerializer(toSerialize.GetType())

📦 Namespace Requirements

You need these using directives:

  • System.IO — for StringWriter, File
  • System.Xml.Serialization — for XmlSerializer

Alternative: Pretty-Printed XML

By default XmlSerializer produces compact XML. If you want indented, human-readable output:

C#
public static string SerializeObject<T>(this T toSerialize)
{
    var serializer = new XmlSerializer(typeof(T));
    var settings = new XmlWriterSettings
    {
        Indent = true,
        OmitXmlDeclaration = false
    };

    using var stringWriter = new StringWriter();
    using var xmlWriter = XmlWriter.Create(stringWriter, settings);

    serializer.Serialize(xmlWriter, toSerialize);
    return stringWriter.ToString();
}
💡 Tip

If you ever need to go the other direction (string → object), the counterpart is xmlSerializer.Deserialize(new StringReader(xmlString)). Symmetrical API, same pattern.

I have a problem with the embedded bitcode term.
What is embedded bitcode?
When to enable, ```ENABLE_BITCODE``` in new Xcode?
What happens to the binary when enabled, ```ENABLE_BITCODE``` in Xcode 7?
cot:
The user is asking about "embedded bitcode" in the context of Xcode and iOS development. They have three specific questions:
1. What is embedded bitcode?
2. When to enable ENABLE_BITCODE in new Xcode?
3. What happens to the binary when enabled in Xcode 7?

Let me provide a comprehensive, well-structured HTML response covering these topics with technical depth.

Key facts:
- Bitcode is an intermediate representation of compiled code (similar to LLVM IR)
- ENABLE_BITCODE was introduced in Xcode 6 (2014) and became default for iOS apps in Xcode 7 (2015)
- When bitcode is embedded, the app binary contains LLVM IR instead of (or alongside) native machine code
- Apple's App Store can re-compile the bitcode into native machine code for newer hardware without requiring app updates
- In Xcode 14+ (2022), bitcode was deprecated and removed
- Bitcode embedding increases binary size but enables future recompilation
- It was used for watchOS and iOS apps
- The binary gets an additional __LLVM section containing the bitcode IR

Let me structure this clearly with cards, tables, callouts, and technical details.
html:
Embedded bitcode is LLVM Intermediate Representation (IR) compiled into your app binary so Apple's App Store can re-compile your app for future hardware without you shipping a new update. ENABLE_BITCODE was the Xcode build setting that controlled this — it was the default in Xcode 7–13, and was fully removed in Xcode 14.

1 · What Is Embedded Bitcode?

The Concept

When you compile an iOS/watchOS app, the toolchain produces two things:

  • Native machine code (ARM64 instructions) — the executable that actually runs on the device.
  • Bitcode (LLVM IR) — a hardware-agnostic, platform-independent intermediate representation embedded in the binary inside a special __LLVM,__bitcode section.

Bitcode is not a runtime format. It is a build-time artifact stored in the Mach-O binary so Apple's servers can re-emit native code for newer CPUs/OS versions.

Why Apple Needed It

  • Apple introduced new CPU micro-architectures faster than developers updated apps.
  • Bitcode let Apple re-compile the LLVM IR on their build farm targeting a new chip (e.g., A10 → A11 → A17) and push the recompiled binary to users without requiring the developer to resubmit.
  • It also enabled app thinning — the App Store could strip unused architectures before delivering to a device.
Analogy

Think of bitcode as shipping the blueprint alongside the finished house. Apple keeps the blueprint so they can rebuild the house to code for a new building standard, even if you never visit again.

2 · What Happens to the Binary (Xcode 7)

Mach-O Section Layout with ENABLE_BITCODE = YES

SectionContentsNotes
__TEXT,__text Native ARM64 machine code What the CPU actually executes
__LLVM,__bitcode LLVM IR (serialized bitcode) Added only when bitcode is enabled
__LLVM,__cmdline Original clang invocation flags Preserves compile options for re-compilation
__LLVM,__stub_group Per-function stubs for re-linking Enables selective recompilation of functions
Binary Size Impact +15 – 40 % Bitcode IR roughly duplicates the code footprint
Link Time Overhead +2 – 10 s Extra LLVM IR emission per TU at link stage
App Store Re-compile ~5 – 15 min Apple's farm recompiles IR → new native binary
Key Constraint in Xcode 7

If ENABLE_BITCODE = YES, every static library, framework, and object file linked into your target must also contain bitcode. Mixing bitcode and non-bitcode binaries produces a linker error: ld: bitcode bundle could not be generated because 'libFoo.a' was built without full bitcode.

3 · When to Enable / Disable ENABLE_BITCODE

Xcode 6

Introduced (2014) — Optional

Default was NO. Apple encouraged enabling it for new projects. Mostly relevant for watchOS, where bitcode was mandatory.

Xcode 7

Default ON for iOS / watchOS (2015)

ENABLE_BITCODE = YES became the default for new targets. Existing projects opened in Xcode 7 inherited their previous value. You could set it to NO per-target or per-project.

Xcode 8 – 13

Stays ON but Apple's use fades

Apple stopped re-compiling bitcode in the App Store (circa 2017–2018) because the overhead outweighed the benefit. The setting remained but had no practical effect for most iOS apps. It still affected watchOS apps.

Xcode 14

Deprecated & Removed (2022)

ENABLE_BITCODE was deprecated in 14.0 and removed in 14.1. Setting it to YES now triggers a warning and is silently ignored. The __LLVM sections are no longer emitted.

Decision Matrix (Historical)

ScenarioRecommendationWhy
New iOS app, Xcode 7–13 YES Default; Apple could re-compile for new chips; watchOS required it
Linking a 3rd-party .a / framework without bitcode NO Linker will fail; vendor didn't compile with -fembed-bitcode
watchOS app (pre-Xcode 14) YES Apple required it; App Store submission rejected without it
CI / build-time optimization matters NO Saves link time and binary size with zero runtime benefit
Xcode 14+ N/A Setting removed; ignored by the compiler

4 · Build-Setting Reference

Xcode Build Setting 
# In Xcode → Build Settings
ENABLE_BITCODE = YES          # Xcode 7–13 (default)
ENABLE_BITCODE = NO           # Disable embedding (Xcode 7–13)
# Xcode 14+: setting removed; has no effect

# Underlying clang flags when YES:
clang -fembed-bitcode \
      -fembed-bitcode-all \
      -fembed-bitcode-marker=...

# Verify in a Mach-O binary:
otool -l MyApp.app/MyApp | grep -A4 "__LLVM"
# Look for sections: __bitcode, __cmdline, __stub_group

Inspecting an Existing Binary

Terminal / CLI 
# Check if bitcode sections exist
otool -l MyBinary | grep __LLVM

# Dump the embedded bitcode IR (decompile to readable LLVM IR)
llvm-dis -o - MyBinary

# See the original clang command line stored in the binary
strings MyBinary | grep "clang"

# Compare size with/without bitcode
ls -la MyBinary_bitcode_on  MyBinary_bitcode_off
Bottom Line

Embedded bitcode was a forward-compatibility mechanism for Apple's hardware pipeline. In modern Xcode (14+) it no longer exists. If you're maintaining a legacy project that must link pre-compiled static libraries without bitcode, the only path forward is to rebuild those libraries from source or set ENABLE_BITCODE = NO (on Xcode ≤ 13). The binary will contain only native machine code and no __LLVM sections.
