html:
Singletons: O Veredito

Singletons não são inerentemente ruins — mas o padrão é frequentemente usado como atalho para global state, e é aí que mora o perigo real. A crítica não é ao conceito "uma instância única", mas à ocultação de dependências e à rigidez de acoplamento que ele introduz quando usado indiscriminadamente.

A afirmação precisa ser decomposta

"Singletons são ruins" é uma generalização imprecisa. O que é genuinamente problemático é: estado global acessível implicitamente por qualquer componente, sem contrato explícito de dependência. Singleton é apenas uma das muitas formas de conseguir isso.

1. Por que foi inventado? O problema original

Em 1994, o Gang of Four (GoF) publicou Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software. Na época, não existiam contêineres de DI, frameworks de injeção, nem convenções amplas de gerenciamento de ciclo de vida. O Singleton resolveu problemas concretos:

Recursos únicos por hardware

Um driver de impressora, um display, um sensor. O OS garante um dispositivo; a classe deve garantir uma instância que o represente.

Coordenação de estado compartilhado

Um connection pool, um cache de sessão, um registry de eventos. Há legitimately um lugar que deve orquestrar esses recursos.

Acesso global sem passar referências

Antes da DI, a alternativa era passar um Config ou Logger por 12 construtores. O Singleton oferecia "acesso em qualquer lugar".

O problema que ele resolveu foi real

"Garantir exatamente uma instância de uma classe e fornecer um ponto global de acesso a ela." (GoF, Cap. 4). Em contextos de hardware, sistemas operacionais e bibliotecas de baixo nível, essa garantia é legítima e necessária.

2. Onde mora o problema (e ele é generalizável?)

A crítica moderna não é "existe uma instância só". A crítica é sobre como a instância é acessada e como ela acopla o sistema. E sim, o problema se generaliza:

Mecanismo Estado global oculto? Dependência visível na interface? Testável com isolamento?
Singleton clássico (getInstance()) Sim Não Difícil
Variável global / static field Sim Não Difícil
Service Locator Parcial Não Média
Singleton via DI container (escopo singleton) Não Sim (construtor) Sim (mock/inject)
Módulo com estado interno (Node require, JS ES module) Parcial Depende Média

Conclusão: O problema não é "uma instância só". O problema é estado global acessível implicitamente. Um objeto com instância única que é injetado explicitamente via construtor não tem o mesmo problema que um Singleton que qualquer classe alcança com Logger.getInstance().

3. Os problemas concretos ao usar Singleton clássico

1

Acoplamento oculto e invisível

Uma classe OrderService que chama PaymentGateway.getInstance() dentro de um método não revela essa dependência em sua interface. O compilador não a vê. O leitor do código não a vê. O gráfico de dependências não a registra. Você só descobre na hora de trocar o gateway.

2

Testabilidade severamente comprometida

Mocks e fakes precisam substituir a instância. Como o Singleton é acessado por static getInstance(), você precisa de hacks: reflexão para resetar o private static field, bibliotecas como Mockito.mockStatic(), ou monkey-patching. Cada teste unitário vira uma guerra contra o estado global.

3

Violação do Single Responsibility Principle

A classe controla seu próprio ciclo de vida além de fazer seu trabalho de domínio. Ela decide quando nasce, como é destruída, e como é acessada. Isso é responsabilidade de um container, não da classe.

4

Fragilidade a mudanças de requisito

"Precisamos de dois pools de conexão, um para escrita e outro para leitura." Com Singleton, você precisa refatorar todos os call sites que assumiam getInstance(). Com DI, você apenas registra duas instâncias e injeta a correta.

5

Problemas de concorrência e ciclo de vida

Lazy initialization + synchronized vira um gargalo. Eager initialization pode não funcionar em ambientes serverless ou com hot-reload. Destruição do Singleton (close, flush) depende de hooks que nem todo runtime oferece.

6

Contaminação em cascata

Um Singleton que é dependido por 47 classes cria um hub invisível. Alterar sua API requer auditar 47 call sites. O sistema ganha um "ponto de fragilidade oculto" que não aparece em diagramas de dependência.

4. Quando Singleton é a escolha certa

Nem toda instância única é um Singleton problemático. O padrão é legítimo quando:

  • A unicidade é uma verdade ontológica do domínio. Um driver de GPU, um terminal de caixa, um clock do sistema. Não há "duas instâncias corretas".
  • O acesso é restrito e a dependência é explícita. Você injeta a instância no construtor de quem precisa dela. O "singleton" é apenas o escopo no container, não um getInstance() global.
  • O objeto é imutável ou funcionalmente stateless. Um MathConstants, um CodecRegistry de configuração. Sem estado mutável, não há problema de concorrência nem de acoplamento comportamental.
  • O escopo de uso é pequeno e controlado. Um framework interno de 5 módulos. O risco de "call sites invisíveis" é baixo.
Sinal de alerta

Se você precisa de getInstance() em mais de um módulo independente, o Singleton está criando acoplamento que seu design não pretende ter. Reavalie.

5. Alternativas viáveis

Dependency Injection (DI)

A alternativa de facto no ecossistema moderno. O objeto é registrado como escopo singleton (ou scoped, ou transient) no container, e injetado explicitamente via construtor ou parâmetro.

Java / Spring
@Component
public class PaymentGateway {
    // NO private static instance
    // NO public static getInstance()
}

@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final PaymentGateway gateway;

    // Injeção explícita: a dependência
    // está VISÍVEL na interface.
    public OrderService(PaymentGateway gateway) {
        this.gateway = gateway;
    }
}

Registry / Composition Root explícito

Em vez de cada classe buscar seu Singleton, um único ponto de composição cria e conecta as instâncias. O "singleton" existe, mas ninguém o alcança por getInstance() — ele é passado.

Python / Composition Root
def build_app():
    gateway = PaymentGateway()      # única instância
    logger  = StructuredLogger()
    orders  = OrderService(gateway, logger)  # injetado
    return orders

# Em qualquer lugar: orders.process(...)
# NUNCA: PaymentGateway.getInstance()

Context objects / Ambient (limitado)

Em Go, por exemplo, context.Context carrega valores por chamada de função. Em Rust, &ctx é passado explicitamente. O "global" existe, mas viaja como parâmetro — a dependência é visível na assinatura.

Módulos com estado encapsulado (JS/TS)

Um módulo ES que exporta export const config = {...} é tecnicamente uma instância única. O problema só aparece se cada consumidor importa direto em vez de receber via parâmetro. Prefira: módulos exportam fábricas, o composition root injeta.

6. Resumo comparativo

Dimensão Singleton clássico Singleton via DI
Dependência visível na interface? Não Sim
Substituível em testes? Não (hack necessário) Sim (mock no construtor)
Quem controla o ciclo de vida? A própria classe O container
Acoplamento visível em diagramas? Não Sim
Unicidade garantida? Sim Sim (escopo singleton)
Múltiplas instâncias futuras? Refatorar call sites Registrar outro bean

7. A regra prática

    // NO public static getInstance()

html:
The apparent contradiction dissolves under scrutiny. Ancient texts record rounded, functional measurements—not metrological proofs of π. Multiple scholarly frameworks (rounding, wall-thickness geometry, and ancient approximation conventions) each independently reconcile 1 Kings 7:23 with π ≈ 3.14159. No single explanation is universally agreed upon, but the tension is far smaller than it first appears.

The Problem, Stated Precisely

1 Kings 7:23 — The Molten Sea

The text gives two numbers:

  • Diameter: 10 cubits (brim to brim)
  • Circumference: 30 cubits (measured by a line/rope)

Applying C = π × D naively yields π = 30/10 = 3, which conflicts with the true value of π ≈ 3.14159.

Resolution Frameworks

1. Rounding of Significant Figures

Ancient construction records used whole-number cubits. Neither measurement was claimed to be exact to many decimal places.

  • If the true diameter were 9.55 cubits (rounded up to 10), then 30 / 9.55 ≈ 3.14.
  • If the true circumference were 31.4 cubits (rounded down to 30), then 31.4 / 10 ≈ 3.14.

A single-cubit rounding error on either dimension produces the "π = 3" artifact. This is the simplest and most widely accepted explanation among both biblical scholars and mathematicians.

2. Inner Diameter vs. Outer Circumference

The molten sea was a thick-walled casting (like a cauldron). The text specifies:

  • 10 cubits = brim to brim (the outer diameter at the rim)
  • 30 cubits = measured by a line wrapped around the outside

2 Chronicles 4:6 uses the word qāw (line/cord), suggesting a rope draped around the exterior surface. If the wall thickness is ~1.5–2 cubits, the outer circumference would be larger than π × inner diameter. Conversely, if 10 cubits is the inner diameter and 30 is the outer circumference, the numbers are perfectly consistent with π ≈ 3.14 plus wall thickness.

3. Ancient Approximation: π ≈ 3 as a Working Value

Several ancient Near Eastern cultures used π ≈ 3 for practical construction:

  • The Babylonian value was 3 (documented on cuneiform tablets).
  • The Egyptian Rhind Papyrus (~1650 BC) uses an effective π of ~3.16.
  • 2 Chronicles 4:6 and the Mishnah (Middot) reference π = 3 for Temple dimensions.

Under this reading, the text is accurately reporting the value used in fabrication. The craftsmen didn't "discover" π = 3; they applied the engineering convention of their era. The text records what was built, not a theorem.

4. The Shape May Not Have Been a Perfect Circle

The Hebrew gōl (round/circular) and the description "brim to brim" could permit a slightly elliptical or scalloped basin. Archaeological evidence from similar ancient vessels (e.g., bronze cauldrons from Samaria, c. 8th c. BC) shows near-circular but not perfectly circular profiles.

A deviation of even 2–3% from a true circle, combined with rounding, fully accounts for the discrepancy.

Key Textual Detail: 1 Kings vs. 2 Chronicles

ReferenceMeasurement GivenWording Nuance
1 Kings 7:23 10 cubits diameter, 30 cubits circumference "a line of thirty cubits measured its circumference" — implies a rope measurement along the outer surface
2 Chronicles 4:6 10 cubits diameter, 30 cubits circumference Uses qāw (cord/line), reinforcing the idea of a physical string wrapped around the vessel, not an abstract geometric calculation
1 Kings 7:26 (context) Wall thickness = one handbreadth (~4 fingers ≈ 18 cm) A thick-walled casting; inner and outer perimeters differ measurably
The Wall-Thickness Calculation

If the outer diameter is 10 cubits and the wall is ~1 handbreadth thick, the inner diameter is roughly 9.6 cubits. An inner circumference of 30 cubits would imply π ≈ 3.125 — within 0.5% of the true value. The numbers are not contradictory; they describe different edges of the same physical object.

What the Text Is Actually Doing

1

Recording, Not Proving

The passage is an inventory specification for a building project, not a mathematics textbook. Ancient builders communicated in round numbers appropriate to a measuring stick.

2

Using Conventional π

Whether the craftsmen used π = 3 or π = 3.14, the recorded dimensions are the rounded outputs of whichever convention they followed. The text faithfully reports the fabrication specs.

3

Preserving Practical Geometry

A rope wrapped around a thick-walled basin gives a circumference that differs from π × (inner diameter). The "contradiction" arises only if we silently assume both numbers refer to the same idealized circle.

Broader Context: Ancient Values of π

Babylonian (~1900 BC)

π = 3

Used in area/volume calculations on clay tablets. The most common value in Mesopotamian engineering.

Egyptian (~1650 BC)

π ≈ 3.16

Rhind Papyrus uses (8/9)² × d² for circle area, implying π ≈ 3.16. More precise but still approximate.

Greek (Archimedes, ~250 BC)

3⅐ < π < 3⅛

First rigorous bounds. Solomon's Temple (~950 BC) predates this by ~700 years.

Bottom Line

There is no genuine contradiction. The verse reports rounded, practical construction measurements for a thick-walled cast basin, consistent with either (a) whole-number rounding, (b) inner-vs-outer geometry, or (c) the standard ancient approximation π ≈ 3. The sea of bronze was, of course, physically constructed. The text tells us how they measured it, not what π equals.

A Note on Reading Ancient Technical Texts

When a modern reader applies C = πD to ancient dimensions, they are importing a post-Greek mathematical framework onto a pre-classical engineering document. The honest question is not "does the Bible get π wrong?" but "what did the author's audience understand these numbers to mean?" In every proposed reading, the answer is: they meant what they said, approximately, and the object fit.

3. `for(reset($broken);$kv = each($broken);) {...}` — Iterating through all key-value pairs.
4. `list(, $this->result) = each($this->cache_data);` — Getting just the value (ignoring key) from the first element.

html:
Replacing the Deprecated each() in PHP 7.2+

The each() function was removed in PHP 8.0. It returned a two-element array [0 => key, 1 => value] for the current internal pointer position, then advanced the pointer. In every case, current(), key(), reset(), list(), or a simple foreach loop replace it with cleaner, faster code.

What each() actually did

each($arr) returned [0 => $currentKey, 1 => $currentValue] (or [key => value, 0 => key, 1 => value] for assoc arrays) and advanced the internal array pointer by one. It returned false when the pointer reached the end. This two-in-one behavior (read + advance) is the key to understanding every replacement below.

Quick Reference Table

Pattern Goal Replacement
each($arr) Get current key + value, advance pointer list($k, $v) = [key($arr), current($arr)]; next($arr);
reset($arr); each($arr); Get first key + value reset($arr); list($k, $v) = [key($arr), current($arr)];
list(, $val) = each($arr); Get first value only $val = current($arr); or reset($arr); $val = current($arr);
for(reset($a); $kv = each($a);) Iterate all pairs foreach ($a as $k => $v)
while (each($arr)) Iterate with limit foreach + break

Your Examples, Translated

Old

Example 1 – First key/value pair

PHP 7.1 (deprecated)
$ar = $o->me;
reset($ar);
list($typ, $val) = each($ar);
New

Example 1 – First key/value pair

PHP 7.2+
$ar = $o->me;
reset($ar);
$typ = key($ar);
$val = current($ar);

Or in one line:

PHP 7.2+
list($typ, $val) = [key($ar), current($ar)];
Old

Example 2 – First pair from assoc array

PHP 7.1 (deprecated)
$out = ['me' => [], 'mytype' => 2, '_php_class' => null];
$expected = each($out);
// $expected = ['me' => [], 0 => 'me', 1 => []]
New

Example 2 – First pair from assoc array

PHP 7.2+
$out = ['me' => [], 'mytype' => 2, '_php_class' => null];
$expected = [key($out) => current($out)];
// $expected = ['me' => []]

If you need the numeric-index form too:

PHP 7.2+
$k = key($out);
$v = current($out);
$expected = [$k => $v, 0 => $k, 1 => $v];
Old

Example 3 – Full iteration

PHP 7.1 (deprecated)
for (reset($broken); $kv = each($broken); ) {
    // $kv[0] = key, $kv[1] = value
}
New

Example 3 – Full iteration

PHP 7.2+
foreach ($broken as $k => $v) {
    // use $k and $v directly
}

If you must keep the $kv array shape:

PHP 7.2+
foreach ($broken as $k => $v) {
    $kv = [0 => $k, 1 => $v];
    // ...
}
Old

Example 4 – First value only

PHP 7.1 (deprecated)
list(, $this->result) = each($this->cache_data);
New

Example 4 – First value only

PHP 7.2+
$this->result = current($this->cache_data);

// or, if you need to ignore the key explicitly:
reset($this->cache_data);
list(, $this->result) = [key($this->cache_data),
                          current($this->cache_data)];
Old

Example 5 – Iterate with limit

PHP 7.1 (deprecated)
$i = 0;
reset($array);
while ( (list($id, $item) = each($array))
        || $i < 30 ) {
    // code
    $i++;
}
New

Example 5 – Iterate with limit

PHP 7.2+
$i = 0;
foreach ($array as $id => $item) {
    // code
    $i++;
    if ($i >= 30) break;
}
// continue past the limit if array is shorter
for (; $i < 30; $i++) {
    // code for the "padding" iterations
    $id = null;
    $item = null;
}

Tip: The original || trick ran the body even after each() returned false, with $id/$item left as their last values. Replicate that with the extra for loop, or simply cap the loop with array_slice():

PHP 7.2+ (cleaner)
foreach (array_slice($array, 0, 30, true) as $id => $item) {
    // code
}

General Decision Guide

1

Are you iterating over the whole array?

Use foreach ($arr as $k => $v). It's faster, safer, and doesn't touch the internal pointer.

2

Do you need just the first (or current) element?

Use current($arr) for the value and key($arr) for the key. Call reset($arr) first if you need the first element.

3

Do you need to advance the pointer manually?

Use next($arr) after reading current()/key(). This is rare; foreach handles it for you.

4

Is the array associative and you need the first pair as [key => val]?

Use [$k => $v] = [$k => $v] — or simply reset($arr); $first = array_slice($arr, 0, 1, true); which returns ['me' => []].

Important Gotchas

Internal Pointer

each(), current(), next(), prev(), reset(), and end() all operate on the internal array pointer. foreach operates on a copy of the array (PHP 7+), so modifying the array inside a foreach is safe.

PHP 8.0+

each() was removed entirely in PHP 8.0. If your code still references it, it will throw a fatal error. The deprecation notice you see in 7.2 is the last warning before removal.

Performance

Replacing each() with foreach is typically 2–4× faster because foreach avoids repeated internal-pointer bookkeeping and doesn't allocate a temporary 4-element array on every iteration.

Edge Case – Empty Array

each([]) returned false. current([]) returns false and key([]) returns null. Guard with if (empty($arr)) or use foreach which simply doesn't execute its body.

$i = 0;
reset($array);
while ( (list($id, $item) = each($array))
        || $i < 30 ) {
    // code
    $i++;
}
New

Example 5 – Iterate with limit

PHP 7.2+
$i = 0;
foreach ($array as $id => $item) {
    // code
    $i++;
    if ($i >= 30) break;
}
// continue past the limit if array is shorter
for (; $i < 30; $i++) {
    // code for the "padding" iterations
    $id = null;
    $item = null;
}

Tip: The original || trick ran the body even after each() returned false, with $id/$item left as their last values. Replicate that with the extra for loop, or simply cap the loop with array_slice():

PHP 7.2+ (cleaner)
foreach (array_slice($array, 0, 30, true) as $id => $item) {
    // code
}

General Decision Guide

1

Are you iterating over the whole array?

Use foreach ($arr as $k => $v). It's faster, safer, and doesn't touch the internal pointer.

2

Do you need just the first (or current) element?

Use current($arr) for the value and key($arr) for the key. Call reset($arr) first if you need the first element.

3

Do you need to advance the pointer manually?

Use next($arr) after reading current()/key(). This is rare; foreach handles it for you.

4

Is the array associative and you need the first pair as [key => val]?

Use [$k => $v] = [$k => $v] — or simply reset($arr); $first = array_slice($arr, 0, 1, true); which returns ['me' => []].

Important Gotchas

Internal Pointer

each(), current(), next(), prev(), reset(), and end() all operate on the internal array pointer. foreach operates on a copy of the array (PHP 7+), so modifying the array inside a foreach is safe.

PHP 8.0+

each() was removed entirely in PHP 8.0. If your code still references it, it will throw a fatal error. The deprecation notice you see in 7.2 is the last warning before removal.

Performance

Replacing each() with foreach is typically 2–4× faster because foreach avoids repeated internal-pointer bookkeeping and doesn't allocate a temporary 4-element array on every iteration.

Edge Case – Empty Array

each([]) returned false. current([]) returns false and key([]) returns null. Guard with if (empty($arr)) or use foreach which simply doesn't execute its body.

instruction: Can someone please give an explanation of different egg preparations?
cot:
The user wants an explanation of different egg preparations. This is a culinary/cooking topic. I should cover the major ways eggs can be prepared, organized in a visually engaging way. Let me think about the best structure:

1. A summary overview
2. Major categories of egg preparations organized logically
3. Key details for each preparation method
4. Maybe a comparison table
5. Tips or callouts for common mistakes

Let me think about the main preparations:
- Scrambled (soft, hard, creamy)
- Fried (sunny-side up, over-easy, over-medium, over-hard, basted)
- Poached
- Boiled (soft, medium, hard, jammy)
- Omelette (French, American, rolled)
- Baked (shirred, in casseroles)
- Custard (French, English, flan)
- Soufflé
- Meringue
- Hollandaise/sauces
- Pickled/cured
- Coddled

I'll organize these into a rich, visual HTML layout with cards, grids, a table, and callouts. Let me make it comprehensive but scannable.
html:
Eggs are the most versatile ingredient in cooking. Nearly every preparation hinges on heat control and coagulation temperature — egg whites set at ~62°C (144°F) and yolks at ~70°C (158°F). Master that range and every method becomes intuitive.

The Major Preparations

🍳 Fried

Cooked in a pan with a thin layer of fat. The yolk remains whole; the white sets around it.

  • Sunny-side up — one side only; yolk stays liquid, white just barely set.
  • Over-easy — flipped once; yolk still runny.
  • Over-medium — flipped; yolk partially thickened, jammy.
  • Over-hard — flipped and cooked through; yolk fully set.
  • Basted / basted-up — spooned hot butter over the top instead of flipping.
Low–Medium Heat

🥚 Scrambled

Yolk and white are broken together, then stirred while cooking. Texture depends on heat and technique.

  • Soft / creamy — low heat, constant slow stirring, removed while still glossy and slightly underdone. Classic French style.
  • Medium / American diner — medium heat, folded into large curds. Slightly drier.
  • Hard / overcooked — high heat, large rubbery curds. Generally discouraged.
  • Tomato-based (shakshuka) — scrambled into a spiced tomato sauce.
Agitation + Heat Control

🥚 Boiled

Cooked in-shell in water. The result is a gradient from liquid to fully set yolk.

  • Soft (3–4 min) — white barely set, yolk completely liquid. For egg cups.
  • Medium / Jammy (6–7 min) — white firm, yolk thick and custardy. The "perfect" texture for ramen, avocado toast, grain bowls.
  • Hard (10–12 min) — both fully set. For deviled eggs, salad, snacking.
  • Coddled — boiled gently in a small jar or cup; yolk stays runny, white barely set.
Time = Texture

🥚 Poached

Cracked into simmering water (or a thin sauce) so the white wraps around a warm, liquid yolk. No shell, no direct heat on the pan surface.

  • Classic poach — 160–180°F water, 3–4 min. Tender white, fully runny yolk.
  • Shirred / baked in sauce — cracked into a ramekin with cream, tomato, or broth and baked until white is just set.
  • Technique tips — fresh eggs hold shape best; a gentle vortex in the water helps wrap the white.
Delicate — Low Temp

🥚 Omelette

Beaten eggs cooked in a pan, folded around a filling or served open.

  • French-style — small, pale, no browning. Interior is creamy/soft. Folded into a cigar shape.
  • American-style — larger, often lightly browned, folded in half with fillings (cheese, ham, peppers).
  • Tortilla española — thick, round, with potato and onion; no fold.
  • Soufflé omelette — whites whipped separately, folded in for a puffy, almost cake-like texture.
Medium–Low Heat

🥚 Baked / Shirred

Eggs cooked dry-heat in an oven, often in a vessel with another ingredient.

  • Shirred eggs — cracked into a ramekin with butter/cream, baked at 350°F until white is set but yolk is still soft.
  • Baked in sauce — poached-then-baked in tomato, béchamel, or mushroom sauce.
  • In casseroles & gratins — as a binder or topping (e.g., eggs over hash, baked into a frittata).
Dry Heat, Even Cooking

Egg-Based Sauces & Emulsions

Hollandaise & Béarnaise

Warm emulsions of egg yolk, butter, and acid. Made by gently cooking yolks over a bain-marie (double boiler) until they thicken, then whisking in melted butter.

Key risk: overheating scrambles the yolks. Stay below 150°F / 65°C.

Custard & Pudding

Yolks thickened with milk/cream and sugar. English custard is stirred to ~75°C; French crème pâtissière adds starch; flan / crème caramel is baked in a water bath until just set.

Key risk: exceeding ~80°C causes curdling / "weeping."

Whipped & Aerated Preparations

Meringue

Egg whites whipped to stiff peaks and baked at low heat. Three types:

  • French — raw whites + sugar, baked until crisp.
  • Swiss — whites + sugar heated over a bain-marie, then whipped.
  • Italian — hot sugar syrup poured into whipping whites.

Soufflé

Flavored base (cheese, chocolate, lemon) enriched with whipped egg whites, baked in a tall dish. The trapped air expands, causing the dramatic rise. Must be served immediately.

Quick-Reference: Temperature & Time

Preparation Temp / Heat Time (approx.) Yolk State
Sunny-side up Low–Med · ~120°C pan 2–3 min Runny / liquid
Over-easy Medium · flip once 2–3 min Runny
Over-hard Medium 5–6 min Fully set
Scrambled (soft) Low · constant stir 4–6 min — (mixed)
Soft boiled Rolling boil · 100°C 3–4 min Liquid
Jammy / medium boiled Rolling boil 6–7 min Thick, custardy
Hard boiled Rolling boil 10–12 min Fully set
Poached Simmer · 75–80°C 3–4 min Warm, runny
French omelette Med-low · no color 2–3 min Creamy interior
Shirred / baked Oven · 175°C / 350°F 8–12 min Soft, just set
Custard (stirred) Bain-marie · 70–80°C 8–12 min Thickened cream
Meringue Low oven · 100–120°C 1–3 hr — (whites)

Common Mistakes & Pro Tips

⚠️ The #1 Egg Mistake: Too Much Heat

Almost every "bad" egg — rubbery scrambled, green-ringed hard-boiled, broken poached, curdled custard — comes from excessive temperature. Egg proteins tighten and squeeze out water once you push past their coagulation range. When in doubt, pull the egg off the heat while it still looks slightly underdone; residual heat finishes the job.

🟢 Green Ring on Hard-Boiled Eggs

Caused by iron in the yolk reacting with sulfur from the white — a sign of overcooking. Fix: shorten boil time, then shock in ice water immediately.

🟢 Poached Egg Falling Apart

Use the freshest eggs possible (the inner white is thicker). Create a gentle vortex in the water and lower the egg in from a small cup. A splash of vinegar helps the white coagulate faster.

🟢 Scrambled Eggs Turn Dry

Cook on low heat, stir slowly, and remove from the pan when the eggs are still glossy and slightly wet. Carryover cooking finishes them. A knob of butter stirred in at the end adds richness.

🟢 Omelette Browning Too Fast

Use a well-seasoned non-stick or carbon steel pan, medium-low heat, and a generous knob of butter. The French omelette should be pale gold, never brown — browning means the heat is too high.

💡 Egg Doneness Ladder (Yolk)

Rare / Runny → ~62°C → Soft / Jammy → ~68°C → Medium / Custardy → ~72°C → Firm / Fully Set → ~78°C+ → Overcooked / Crumbly. Every preparation on this page is essentially a way to land the yolk somewhere on this ladder.

Stepper: Choosing the Right Method

1

Do you want the yolk runny or set?

Runny → poach, sunny-side up, soft boil. Set → hard boil, over-hard, omelette, scrambled.

2

Wet heat or dry heat?

Water-based methods (poach, boil, coddle) give gentler, more even cooking. Fat-based methods (fry, omelette, scramble) add flavor and browning.

3

Whites only, yolks only, or whole?

Separating eggs opens up meringue, soufflé, hollandaise, and custard. Whole-egg methods are simpler and more everyday.

4

Plating & pairing

Poached → over a Benedict or grain bowl. Jammy boiled → avocado toast, ramen. Soft scramble → on toast with herbs. Omelette → stuffed with cheese, herbs, or vegetables.

instruction:
I'm running a relatively small one-man business in the software sector. I just started and am trying to create a larger portfolio. For that, I offer some friends free services. 
I found a few reasons to send these clients €0,- invoices, mostly similar to the reasons to send 100% discount invoices to charity funds that I gave here:

* Clarity about what has to be done and when 
* No transfers (as I would have with a 0% discount bill and returning the money as a gift)

And also:

* With an invoice I have more distinguishable clients which makes that I have more chance on getting a better certificate from the state (doesn't matter how it exactly works, this is an advantage)

Suppose that these clients won't have a problem with the €0,- invoices, could there be any reason for me to not send them?
I ask this, because I've never seen people sending invoices like this, and I can only see advantages.
cot:
The user is a one-man software business in what appears to be a German-speaking European country (mentions "certificate from the state" which sounds like it could be German "Gewerbe" related, or Dutch "Belastingdienst", or similar). They want to send €0 invoices to friends for free services. They've identified advantages and want to know potential disadvantages or reasons NOT to do this.

Let me think about this carefully:

1. **Tax implications**: Even a €0 invoice creates a taxable transaction. In many EU countries (Germany, Netherlands, Belgium, etc.), you must still file VAT (Umsatzsteuer/BTW) on the invoice even if the amount is €0. The invoice must show VAT rates. If you're below the Kleinunternehmer threshold in Germany, this might not matter. But if you're VAT-registered, you need to handle it.

2. **VAT/Invoice compliance**: A €0 invoice is unusual. In Germany, the Umsatzsteuergesetz requires invoices to show the consideration (Entgelt). A €0 invoice might be questioned by tax authorities. In the Netherlands, a 0% discount invoice is actually common and accepted.

3. **Business registration/licensing**: Having "clients" on paper could affect your business registration status, insurance requirements, or professional licenses.

4. **Liability**: An invoice implies a contractual relationship. If something goes wrong with the service, you have a paper trail that could be used against you. A €0 invoice still establishes a legal relationship.

5. **Accounting complexity**: You need to track these, file them, potentially include them in your tax returns. For a €0 transaction, this is administrative overhead.

6. **The "certificate from the state" point**: This sounds like it could be related to German "Kleinunternehmerregelung" or some kind of professional certification. The user says it gives them more distinguishable clients. This is a valid point in some jurisdictions.

7. **Potential tax authority scrutiny**: Tax authorities might question why you're invoicing at €0. It could look like you're trying to manipulate your revenue figures, or it could raise questions about whether these are truly "business" transactions vs. personal favors.

8. **In some jurisdictions**: A €0 invoice might not be legally valid as an invoice. The definition of an invoice requires a "consideration" or "payment claim."

I have thought about this long enough; time to give my answer.
html:
Sending €0 Invoices to Friends: The Short Answer

You can send €0 invoices in most EU jurisdictions, and for a small software business the administrative burden is manageable. However, there are several legal, tax, and practical risks that make it not a purely advantageous move. Below is a structured breakdown of what you should verify before sending them.

⚠️ Important Disclaimer

This is general information, not tax or legal advice. Rules differ significantly between Germany (Umsatzsteuergesetz), Netherlands (BTW), Belgium, Austria, etc. The points below are broad EU-wide considerations. Consult your local tax advisor before adopting this practice.

1 · Tax & VAT Compliance

🔍 VAT on a €0 Invoice

A €0 invoice is not the same as "no transaction." In most EU countries, the invoice must still display:

  • VAT rate (e.g., 19% / 21%)
  • A line item with €0 net + €0 VAT
  • Your VAT ID / tax number

You must include it in your VAT return (Umsatzsteuer-Voranmeldung / BTW-aangifte). Even with €0, the transaction is reported. If you are a Kleinunternehmer (Germany) or below the BTW threshold (NL), this is simpler — but you still need to file.

📋 Is a €0 Invoice "Valid"?

This is the most debated point:

  • Germany: §14 UStG requires an "Entgelt" (consideration). A €0 amount is technically a consideration of zero. Tax authorities generally accept 100%-discount invoices, but a flat €0 with no discount reference can look like a "non-transaction" and may be queried.
  • Netherlands: €0 invoices are explicitly recognized (e.g., for 100% korting). This is well-established practice.
  • Other jurisdictions: Varies. Some require a non-zero "basis" amount.

Tip: Instead of writing "€0," consider writing "100% discount" on a normal invoice. It produces the same €0 total but is far more defensible under invoice regulations.

💡 Practical Tip: Invoice Format

Structure the line item as:

Service description …… € 500,00
Discount 100% …… – € 500,00
Total …… € 0,00
VAT (19%) …… € 0,00

This shows a real "value" was rendered, the discount was applied, and the net is €0. It reads as a genuine business transaction rather than a placeholder.

2 · Legal & Liability Exposure

📜 An Invoice Creates a Contract

The moment you send an invoice, you create a documented business relationship. This has consequences:

  • Warranty / liability: Your friends are now "clients." If your software breaks, you may be held to professional standards (Gewährleistung, warranty obligations) rather than informal "helping a friend" expectations.
  • Terms & conditions: An invoice typically references T&Cs. If you haven't written any, the default statutory terms apply — which are often stricter than what you'd agree with a friend informally.
  • GDPR / data processing: If you handle their data, the invoice formalises a data-processing relationship that triggers GDPR obligations (DPA, records, etc.).
🚨 The Hidden Risk

A €0 invoice does not reduce your liability — it increases it. You are now a professional service provider to these people, with the full legal weight that carries. If a friend's business suffers a loss because of your software, the invoice is evidence of a professional engagement, not a casual favour.

3 · Tax Authority Scrutiny

🏷️ "Are these really clients?"

A tax auditor reviewing your books may ask: Why do you have 12 clients but zero revenue? This can trigger questions about:

  • Whether your activity is a genuine business or a hobby
  • Whether the "clients" are actually friends in a private capacity
  • Whether you're structuring things to avoid reporting income

📊 Income Tax / Gewerbesteuer

€0 transactions produce €0 revenue, so they don't inflate your income tax. However:

  • Your expense-to-revenue ratio looks worse (you have costs but no offsetting income).
  • Some tax offices use revenue as a signal for whether your "Gewerbe" is active. A string of €0 invoices might look like a dormant business, which could affect your registration status.

📄 Documentation Burden

Every invoice you issue must be:

  • Stored for 10 years (Germany) / 7 years (NL)
  • Included in your bookkeeping
  • Reflectable in your annual tax return

For a one-person shop, this is manageable — but it is additional admin for zero monetary return.

4 · The "State Certificate" Argument

🏛️ Client Count & Professional Standing

You mention that having distinguishable clients improves your chances with a state certificate (possibly Handwerkskammer, IHK, Kammer, or a professional qualification body). This is a legitimate strategic advantage in several jurisdictions:

  • Some certification bodies count number of distinct engagements, not revenue.
  • References / testimonials from "clients" carry weight.
  • A portfolio of named projects is more impressive than "I helped some friends."

However: If the certificate body audits your invoices and finds them all at €0, this may undermine the impression of a functioning business. You may need at least a few paid engagements to look credible.

5 · When €0 Invoices Make Sense vs. When They Don't

Scenario€0 Invoice OK?Reason
One-off small service for a friendYesLow risk, easy to explain, builds portfolio
Recurring / ongoing service (maintenance, hosting)CautionImplies an ongoing business relationship with liability and admin overhead
Service involving personal data (GDPR-relevant)RiskyFormalises a data-processing contract; DPA required
Service that could cause business loss to the friendRiskyProfessional liability applies; no "I was just helping" defence
You are Kleinunternehmer (no VAT)YesNo VAT reporting complication; just file the invoice
You are VAT-registeredManageableMust include in VAT return; use "100% discount" format
You want the invoice purely for "client count" on paperQuestionableMay look artificial to auditors; better to charge a token amount (€5–€20)

6 · Alternatives Worth Considering

💶 Token Invoice (€1 – €25)

Charge a small, symbolic amount. This:

  • Is unambiguously a "real" business transaction
  • Looks natural to tax authorities and certification bodies
  • Still keeps cost effectively zero for your friends
  • Avoids the "is this a real invoice?" debate

Even a €5 invoice is trivially easy to explain and is bulletproof from a compliance standpoint.

📝 Written Agreement / LOI Instead

If the goal is purely clarity of scope and deadlines (one of your stated reasons), a project brief or letter of intent achieves the same thing without triggering any invoice/tax machinery.

For the "client count" advantage, you can still reference these engagements in your portfolio without a formal invoice.

7 · Bottom Line

1

Confirm your jurisdiction's rules

Ask your tax advisor (or Steuerberater / belastingadviseur) specifically: "Can I issue a €0 invoice, and does it need to be reported in my VAT/income return?" One 15-minute call saves months of uncertainty.

2

Prefer "100% discount" over flat €0

If you go the invoice route, structure it as a normal invoice with a 100% discount line. It is legally cleaner in nearly every EU country and avoids the "non-transaction" interpretation.

3

Limit liability exposure

If you invoice, add a short clause or side-letter clarifying the engagement is pro bono, limited in scope, and that no professional warranty beyond what you personally agree applies. Have your friends acknowledge this in writing.

4

Consider a small paid engagement for credibility

For your state-certificate goal, a mix of a few token-paid invoices (€10–€50) plus a few €0 looks far more natural than an entire portfolio of zero-value engagements.

✅ Final Verdict

html:
PHP Error Handling: You're Not Alone in the Confusion

Short Answer

These three methods are not interchangeable. They operate at different architectural levels, have different recovery semantics, and were designed for fundamentally different purposes. PHP's error handling evolved across 20+ years, which is why the manual shows all three — but modern PHP (7.4+, 8.x) has a clear preferred path.

The confusion is legitimate. PHP accumulated error mechanisms across versions without a unified design. However, the modern answer is straightforward: use throw for application-level errors, let PHP's internal error reporting handle language-level errors, and reserve die()/exit() for fatal bootstrap scenarios only.

The Three Styles — What They Actually Do

Legacy / Fatal

die() / exit()

Mechanism: Immediately terminates the script. No stack unwinding. No finally. No catch. The process is over.

Recovery: None. Not catchable. Not recoverable.

Best for: Bootstrap failures (DB connection dead at startup, missing critical config). You literally cannot proceed.

Structured / Catchable

throw new Exception

Mechanism: Creates an object with a message, code, stack trace, and file/line metadata. Walks up the call stack looking for a try/catch.

Recovery: Full. Catchable, loggable, convertible, re-throwable.

Best for: Application-level errors, domain logic failures, library boundaries.

Middleware / Handler

trigger_error()

Mechanism: Injects a user-level error (E_USER_ERROR/WARNING/NOTICE) into PHP's error pipeline. Goes through set_error_handler().

Recovery: Partial. Not catchable by try/catch. Interceptable by a registered error handler. Can be converted to exception via handler.

Best for: Framework-internal diagnostics, deprecated API warnings, non-fatal operational issues.

Are They Drop-in Replacements? NO

Capability die()/exit() throw trigger_error()
Catchable by try/catch ❌ No ✅ Yes ❌ No (unless handler converts it)
Carries stack trace ❌ No ✅ Yes ❌ No
Can carry error code ❌ No ✅ Yes (int code) ⚠️ Via constant level only
Custom error type (class hierarchy) ❌ No ✅ Yes (extends Exception) ❌ No
Script continues after handling ❌ Script dies ✅ Yes ⚠️ E_USER_ERROR halts; WARNING/NOTICE continue
Works with finally blocks ❌ No ✅ Yes ❌ No
Interoperable with frameworks (Laravel, Symfony) ⚠️ Breaks them ✅ Native ⚠️ Intercepted but awkward
Critical Distinction: trigger_error(E_USER_ERROR) ≠ throw

Despite the name "ERROR," E_USER_ERROR does not throw an exception. It calls your error handler (if registered) and then terminates the script. It does not unwind the stack, does not trigger finally, and cannot be caught by try/catch. This surprises many developers.

What Modern PHP (8.x) Actually Gives You

PHP 7 made a critical change: engine-level errors became throwable objects. This unified two of the three styles.

Pre-PHP 7

  • mysql_connect() returned false on failure
  • Warnings/notices were not exceptions
  • You had to check return values manually

PHP 7+ / 8+

  • PDO::connect() throws on failure
  • TypeError, ValueError, DivisionByZeroError are real exceptions
  • trigger_error() still exists but is rarely needed
PHP 8 — Modern Connection Handling
// No die(), no manual check — PDO throws natively
try {
    $pdo = new PDO('mysql:host=localhost;dbname=app', 'root', 'pass', [
        PDO::ATTR_ERRMODE => PDO::ERRMODE_EXCEPTION, // throws on query errors too
    ]);
} catch (PDOException $e) {
    // Structured, catchable, loggable, recoverable
    error_log($e->getMessage());
    // Decide: retry? fallback? graceful degradation?
    http_response_code(503);
    exit('Service temporarily unavailable'); // exit() here is for HTTP layer, not error handling
}

Decision Framework: Which Style, When?

1

Is the script fundamentally unable to continue?

die() / exit() — but only at the outermost bootstrap boundary (index.php entry point, CLI script main). Never inside a function or class method.

2

Is this an application/domain error that callers should handle?

throw new CustomException(...) — with a typed exception class hierarchy. This is your default choice for 90% of cases.

3

Is this a framework-level diagnostic or deprecation warning?

trigger_error(..., E_USER_DEPRECATED) — used by libraries to warn consumers without breaking them. Symfony and Laravel use this internally.

4

Is this an engine-level problem (type mismatch, undefined index)?

Do nothing manually. Let PHP throw its built-in TypeError / ValueError. Catch at the boundary.

A Proper Exception Architecture

PHP — Typed Exception Hierarchy
// Domain exceptions — your application's language
abstract class AppException extends Exception {}

class DatabaseConnectionException extends AppException {}
class ConfigurationException       extends AppException {}
class PaymentGatewayException       extends AppException {}

// At the boundary (controller / CLI entry):
try {
    $order = $service->processPayment($cart);
} catch (PaymentGatewayException $e) {
    // Specific recovery: retry with backup gateway
    $order = $backupGateway->process($cart);
} catch (AppException $e) {
    // Generic fallback: log + 500
    $logger->error($e->getMessage(), ['trace' => $e->getTraceAsString()]);
    http_response_code(500);
} catch (Throwable $e) {
    // Catch-all for engine errors (TypeError, ValueError, etc.)
    // In production: never expose details to client
    $logger->critical((string)$e);
    http_response_code(500);
}
Why This Beats die() and trigger_error()

Typed exceptions let you match on error type, carry structured context (order ID, gateway name), compose error messages, and test error paths in unit tests. You cannot do any of this with die('Could not connect').

Why the Manual Shows All Three

Historical Layers

PHP's error handling was built incrementally:

  • PHP 3–4: die(), warnings, notices — no exceptions
  • PHP 5: Exception class introduced (2000)
  • PHP 7: Error interface, engine errors become throwable
  • PHP 8: TypeError, ValueError, enums, strict typing

The manual documents all layers because some still exist for backward compatibility.

The mysql_*_ Example You Quoted

The mysql_connect() example is deprecated since PHP 7.0 and removed since PHP 8.0. It's a fossil in the manual. The modern equivalent (PDO, mysqli) uses exceptions natively.

If you see die('Could not connect') in a tutorial, it's teaching you an antipattern from 2009.

Quick Reference: The Modern Default

Default for app logic throw Typed exceptions, catchable, testable
Default for engine errors Throwable PHP throws them for you (PHP 7+)
Default for bootstrap exit() Only at the outermost entry point
trigger_error() Rare Framework internals, deprecation warnings only
One Practical Tip: Convert trigger_error to Exceptions

If you're stuck in a legacy codebase that uses trigger_error(), you can bridge them:

PHP — Bridge Error Handler → Exceptions
set_error_handler(function (int $errno, string $errstr, ?string $file, ?int $line) {
    // Convert E_USER_WARNING / E_USER_NOTICE into catchable exceptions
    throw new ErrorException($errstr, 0, $errno, $file ?? '', $line ?? 0);
});

// Now this legacy call:
trigger_error('Config missing key "db_host"', E_USER_WARNING);

// ...becomes catchable:
try {
    trigger_error('Config missing key "db_host"', E_USER_WARNING);
} catch (ErrorException $e) {
    $logger->warning($e->getMessage());
}

The Honest Verdict

You're right that the options are excessive. PHP's design by committee across 25 years produced a layered,

Changing Author & Committer Name/Email for Multiple Commits

Git stores author (who wrote the code) and committer (who applied the commit) as separate fields. You can rewrite either — or both — for a range of commits using rebase --exec, filter-repo, or filter-branch. html:
Emergency Signalling for Remote Solo Hiking

A flare gun is no longer the best option for your scenario. A PLB (Personal Locator Beacon) combined with a satellite communicator and a handful of hand-held flares as a visual backup gives you layered, modern, and more reliable coverage. Below is a full breakdown.

⚠ Solo + No Cell Service = Zero Margin for Error

With no partner to relay a message or flag you missing, your signalling device is the only link between an emergency and a rescue. Treat this purchase as the single most important item in your pack, above boots, above shelter, above food.

1. The Modern Replacement: Personal Locator Beacons (PLBs)

What a PLB Actually Is

A PLB is a small, handheld transmitter that sends a 406 MHz distress signal to the Cospas-Sarsat satellite network (operated jointly by the US, EU, Russia, and others). The signal includes your GPS position and a unique 15-digit hex ID tied to your registration, which includes your emergency contacts and itinerary.

Activation is a single button. The beacon pings every ~50 seconds for up to 48+ hours. Rescue coordination centres (RCCs) receive the alert within 15–60 minutes and dispatch SAR assets.

Why It Beats a Flare Gun

  • Works in fog, rain, night, dense canopy — a flare's visible range collapses to near zero in bad weather; a radio signal doesn't care.
  • Transmits your exact coordinates — a flare tells rescuers a direction; a PLB tells them a point.
  • Triggers a formal, tracked SAR response — a flare is an unstructured visual cue; a PLB opens an official incident file.
  • 48+ hour broadcast window — you can be unconscious, injured, or hidden and the beacon keeps transmitting.
  • ~150–250 g, pocket-sized — lighter than most flare guns.
Registration is mandatory (in most countries)

In the US, register with NOAA (free). In the UK, with the MRCC. In Australia, with AMSA. Your registration links the beacon's hex ID to your emergency contacts, planned route, and medical info — so rescuers know who you are before they arrive. A flare gun has no equivalent.

2. Two-Way Satellite Communicators (the "check-in + SOS" hybrid)

A satellite communicator lets you send text messages, track your breadcrumb trail, and trigger an SOS over Iridium or Globalstar satellite constellations — no cell towers needed. You can send a "I'm fine, ETA 6 pm" message to your family and activate a distress alert from the same device.

Device SOS Path Two-Way Messaging Weight Subscription Notes
Garmin inReach Mini 2 GEOS (24/7 dispatch) Text via Iridium 9601 ~100 g ~$15–$65/mo Best all-rounder; small, rugged, 10-day battery
Garmin inReach Messenger GEOS Text + limited data ~150 g ~$15–$65/mo Longer battery (~30 days), slightly bulkier
Zoleo GEOS Text via Globalstar ~130 g ~$10–$60/mo Simple interface; Globalstar coverage slightly narrower in very high latitudes
SPOT Gen4 Boston Globe / GEOS One-way messages only ~125 g ~$12–$50/mo Cheapest entry; no two-way texting
✅ Why this matters for a solo hike

A PLB is fire-and-forget: you press the button and wait. A satellite communicator lets you update rescuers on your condition ("ankle is broken, can't walk, 2 km from the trailhead") so SAR teams arrive with the right equipment, helicopter vs. ground team, medical kit, etc. That can cut rescue time from hours to minutes of decision-making at the RCC.

3. Where Flares Still Belong (as a visual layer)

Hand-Held Flares — not a flare gun

A flare gun (single-shot or 3-shot pistol-style) is heavy, has limited ammo, requires a licence in many jurisdictions, and is only useful if a search aircraft is already overhead and needs a visual fix. For your scenario, a flare gun is a poor primary tool.

However, 2–3 hand-held marine-style flares (e.g., USCG-approved SOLAS hand-held red flares, ~$15–25 each) are worth carrying in a zip-lock bag because:

  • They give you a visible signal to a passing aircraft, vehicle, or hiker when you're close enough to be seen but too far to shout.
  • They work when a satellite device is dead, wet, or you forgot to turn it on.
  • They are zero-subscription, zero-registration, zero-battery.

Check your national and local regulations: in many US states, carrying a hand-held flare without a licence is legal, but a flare gun may require a permit. In the UK, Australia, and EU, flare guns are regulated weapons.

4. The Recommended Layered Kit

1

Primary: PLB (406 MHz)

One of these: ACR ResQLink 400, McMurdo Fastfind Plus 222, or Ocean Signal rescueME PLB1. Register it. Test annually. This is your last-resort, works-anywhere, 48-hour distress beacon. ~$300–$450, no subscription.

2

Secondary: Satellite Communicator

Garmin inReach Mini 2 (or Messenger). Daily check-ins, breadcrumb tracking shared with family, and a second SOS path through GEOS. ~$350–$400 hardware + subscription. Gives you two independent rescue channels.

3

Visual Backup: 2–3 Hand-Held Flares

USCG/SOLAS hand-held red flares in a waterproof pouch. Use for signalling a nearby vehicle, boat, or aircraft when you're within ~1–3 km visual range. Cheap insurance against a dead battery.

4

Low-Tech Layer: Whistle + Mirror + Bright Gear

A pealess whistle (louder, works when you can't blow hard), a signal mirror, and high-visibility jacket (orange/yellow). These cost under $15 total and work when every electronic device is dead.

5

Pre-Trip: File a Plan

Leave a detailed itinerary (trail, campsites, water sources, daily checkpoints) with a trusted person and with local park/ranger authorities. If you miss a check-in, SAR is alerted before you even press a beacon button. This is the single most effective "device" you can carry.

5. PLB vs. Flare Gun vs. Satellite Messenger — At a Glance

Criterion Flare Gun PLB Satellite Messenger
Works in fog / night / rain ❌ Poor ✅ Yes ✅ Yes
Transmits GPS position ❌ No ✅ Yes ✅ Yes
Triggers formal SAR dispatch ❌ No (informal) ✅ Yes (Cospas-Sarsat) ✅ Yes (GEOS dispatch)
Two-way comms ❌ No ❌ No ✅ Yes
Battery / power dependency ❌ Single shot ✅ 48+ hrs ⚠️ Days–weeks
Subscription cost None None ~$15–65/mo
Weight in pack ~600–800 g + ammo ~150–250 g ~100–150 g
Legal / licensing ⚠️ Often restricted ✅ Free registration ✅ None
Cost (hardware) ~$100–$250 ~$300–$450 ~$350–$400

6. Practical Tips for Your Specific Trip

Before You Go

  • Register your PLB and update it with your exact route, emergency contacts, and any medical conditions (allergies, medications).
  • Share your breadcrumb trail live via the satellite messenger so family can see your progress without you messaging.
  • File a plan with the land manager (USFS, NPS, state park, or equivalent). Ask them to initiate a SAR alert if you miss your planned exit by a set window.
  • Test your PLB — most have a test mode (short 1-second burst) you can run at home. Do this annually.

On the Trail

  • Carry the PLB and messenger on your person (hip belt or chest strap), not buried in your pack. If you're unconscious and your pack is 10 m away, the beacon is useless.
  • Keep devices in a zip-lock or dry bag inside your pack as a secondary location.
  • Know your GPS coordinates even without a device — carry a paper topo map and know how to read it.
  • Set a daily check-in time and tell your emergency contact who to call if you miss it (local sheriff, ranger station, SAR group).
  • Carry a small first-aid kit, emergency blanket, and headlamp — survival before rescue is a separate problem.
🔁 Redundancy Is the Whole Point

No single device is fail-safe. A PLB battery can die. A satellite messenger can get wet. A flare is one shot. The reason you carry all four layers (PLB → satellite messenger → hand-held flares → whistle/mirror) is that any single failure still leaves you with a working distress path. For a solo trip with no cell coverage, this layering is not paranoia — it is the minimum responsible kit.

Cospas-Sarsat alert time 15–60 min Satellite detection

Battery / power dependency ❌ Single shot ✅ 48+ hrs ⚠️ Days–weeks
Subscription cost None None ~$15–65/mo
Weight in pack ~600–800 g + ammo ~150–250 g ~100–150 g
Legal / licensing ⚠️ Often restricted ✅ Free registration ✅ None
Cost (hardware) ~$100–$250 ~$300–$450 ~$350–$400

6. Practical Tips for Your Specific Trip

Before You Go

Register your PLB

and update it with your exact route, emergency contacts, and any medical conditions (allergies, medications).

Share your breadcrumb trail live

via the satellite messenger so family can see your progress without you messaging.

File a plan with the land manager

(USFS, NPS, state park, or equivalent). Ask them to initiate a SAR alert if you miss your planned exit by a set window.

Test your PLB

most have a test mode (short 1-second burst) you can run at home. Do this annually.

On the Trail

Carry the PLB and messenger on your person

(hip belt or chest strap), buried in your pack. If you're unconscious and your pack is 10 m away, the beacon is useless.

Keep devices in a zip-lock or dry bag

inside your pack as a secondary location.

Know your GPS coordinates

even without a device — carry a paper topo map and know how to read it.

Set a daily check-in time

and tell your emergency contact if you miss it (local sheriff, ranger station, SAR group).

Carry a small first-aid kit, emergency blanket, and headlamp

survival before rescue is a separate problem.

🔁 Redundancy Is the Whole Point

No single device is fail-safe. A PLB battery can die. A satellite messenger can get wet. A flare is one shot. The reason you carry all four layers (PLB → satellite messenger → hand-held flares → whistle/mirror) is that any single failure still leaves you with a working distress path. For a solo trip with no cell coverage, this layering is not paranoia — it is the minimum responsible kit.

Cospas-Sarsat alert time 15–60 min Satellite detection

instruction:
Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof; or abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press; or the right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the Government for a redress of grievances.

I don't understand the part marked in bold.
Congress shall make no law prohibiting the free exercise of religion. So congress should not make a law which prohibits the freedom of religion. I get it.
But Congress shall make a law which respects an establishment of religion. Doesn't "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion" mean congress should not make a law that respects religion because there's "no" in it??
cot:
The user is confused about the First Amendment's Establishment Clause. They're parsing the grammar incorrectly. Let me break down their confusion:

They think:
- "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion" = "Congress shall make a law which respects an establishment of religion"

This is wrong. The correct parsing is:
- "Congress shall make no law [respecting an establishment of religion]"
- "no" negates the entire verb phrase "shall make any law"
- "respecting an establishment of religion" is a prepositional phrase modifying "law" — it describes WHAT kind of law is prohibited

The structure is: "Congress shall make NO LAW [of type X]" where X = "respecting an establishment of religion"

It's NOT: "Congress shall make [NO LAW] [respecting an establishment of religion]" where "no" modifies "respecting"

Let me think about how to explain this clearly. The key grammatical point is:

"make no law respecting X" = "make no law that pertains to X" = "do not make any law concerning X"

The word "no" is not negating "respecting" — it's negating "make any law." The phrase "respecting an establishment of religion" is an adjective modifying "law" (i.e., a law that pertains to the establishment of religion).

So the meaning is: Congress cannot make any law that has anything to do with establishing a religion.

I should use clear examples, maybe analogies, and break down the grammar visually. Let me use cards, maybe a stepper for the parsing, and a callout for the key insight.

Let me structure this as:
1. Summary card - the core misconception
2. Grammar breakdown showing how to parse the sentence
3. Analogy to make it click
4. What it actually means vs what they thought it means
5. Maybe a table comparing the two readings

Let me make this visually clear and punchy.
html:
Your confusion is completely understandable — it's a 18th-century grammar trap. The "no" does not negate "respecting." It negates "make any law." The phrase "respecting an establishment of religion" is just a description of what kind of law is banned.

The Misreading vs. The Correct Reading

❌ How you're parsing it

Congress shall make a law that does not respect an establishment of religion.

Here "no" is treated as negating the word respecting, as if the sentence says: "Don't respect religion."

✅ How the sentence actually works

Congress shall make no law [that pertains to the establishment of religion].

Here "no" negates the verb phrase "shall make any law." The word respecting is not being negated — it's an adjective describing which law is banned.

Grammar Dissection

1

Find the verb being negated

The core clause is "Congress shall make no law." That's the whole action: Congress is forbidden from creating any law. Period. The "no" attaches to law, not to respecting.

2

Identify the modifier

"Respecting an establishment of religion" is a prepositional phrase acting as an adjective. It answers the question: What kind of law? A law concerning the establishment of religion.

3

Put it together

Congress is prohibited from making any law that touches, pertains to, or deals with establishing a religion. "Respecting" here means "pertaining to" — an older usage common in legal English.

The word "respecting" ≠ "showing respect to"

In 18th-century English, "respecting" simply meant "concerning" or "pertaining to." Think of it like the modern phrase "with respect to." It has nothing to do with reverence or honor.

A Modern Analogy That Should Make It Click

18th-Century Legal PhrasePlain English Paraphrase
"Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion." "Congress shall make no law concerning the establishment of religion."
"No law respecting taxes shall apply." "No law about taxes shall apply."
"No law respecting speech shall apply." "No law about speech shall apply."
Simplest test

Try replacing "respecting" with "concerning" everywhere. The whole amendment instantly makes sense:

"Congress shall make no law concerning the establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof; or abridging the freedom of speech…"

Every clause follows the same pattern: "no law [concerning / about / pertaining to] X."

What the Establishment Clause Actually Forbids

✅ Allowed

Individuals freely practicing any religion (or none). Congress can even accommodate religious practices in general law.

❌ Forbidden

Creating a state-sponsored church. Mandating a specific religion. Funding one denomination over others. Writing prayers into public law.

⚖️ The Balance

Government must stay neutral — it can neither establish a religion (this clause) nor suppress religious practice (the next clause).

Why the old grammar is confusing

Modern English rarely uses "respecting" as a standalone adjective meaning "concerning." The Founders wrote in a legal register where respecting = pertaining to. That archaic sense is the entire source of the misunderstanding. You weren't reading it wrong logically — you were reading a dead usage of the word.

instruction: Why are people unwilling to share information about their salary?
cot:
The user is asking about why people are unwilling to share salary information. This is a social/psychological/economic question. Let me think about the various reasons people resist sharing salary information and organize them into a comprehensive, well-structured response.

Key reasons include:
1. Social comparison anxiety - fear of judgment, envy, or status implications
2. Power dynamics - employer pressure, NDAs, workplace culture
3. Cultural taboos - money as private, class sensitivity
4. Negotiation disadvantage - revealing salary weakens bargaining position
5. Relational dynamics - jealousy, resentment, pity in friendships/families
6. Legal/contractual restrictions - salary transparency policies, NDAs
7. Identity and self-worth - salary as proxy for value, vulnerability
8. Practical concerns - safety, fraud risk
9. Gender and equity dynamics - women often face more pushback
10. Psychological factors - loss aversion, social comparison theory

Let me structure this as a rich, multi-dimensional exploration using cards, grids, callouts, steppers, and tables. I'll make it visually engaging and information-dense.
html:
The Salary Taboo: Why People Guard Their Pay

Salary secrecy isn't irrational—it's a deeply layered behavior shaped by social psychology, power structures, cultural norms, and legal frameworks. People withhold pay information because every disclosure carries a cascade of social, economic, and emotional consequences.

Key Statistic

A 2023 Glassdoor survey found 68% of employees would not disclose their salary to a coworker, and 52% wouldn't tell even a close friend. The reluctance spans every industry and seniority level.

1. The Psychological Core

Social Comparison

Salary is one of the most visible proxies for social status. Revealing it triggers upward comparison (feeling inferior) or downward comparison (triggering guilt or resentment in the other person). Festinger's Social Comparison Theory shows that people evaluate themselves against peers—salary makes that evaluation instant and public.

Identity & Self-Worth

Many people conflate their income with their value. Sharing a number feels like exposing a verdict on one's competence, ambition, or worthiness. Lower-than-expected pay can feel like a public admission of failure; higher-than-expected pay can feel like bragging.

Loss Aversion & Vulnerability

People fear that disclosure will cost them something: negotiating power, relationships, respect, or emotional safety. Prospect theory shows losses weigh roughly 2× more than equivalent gains—so the perceived downside of sharing dwarfs any upside.

2. Workplace & Power Dynamics

Employer Control & Legal Barriers

Salary secrecy is often engineered by employers, not just chosen by workers.

MechanismHow It Suppresses Disclosure
Non-Disclosure AgreementsContractual clauses explicitly prohibit discussing compensation with colleagues. Violation risks termination.
Pay Secrecy PoliciesSome companies formally discourage or forbid salary comparisons, framing pay as a "private matter."
Retaliation FearEven where legally protected (e.g., U.S. NLRA §7, UK Equality Act), employees fear being labeled "troublemakers" or losing advancement opportunities.
Performance-Linked PayBonuses, equity, and variable comp make salary feel like a personal performance scorecard rather than a market rate.
Legal Nuance

In the United States, the National Labor Relations Act protects employees' right to discuss wages. However, many workers are unaware of this protection, and employers routinely enforce informal taboos. As of 2024, 23 U.S. states have enacted salary transparency laws requiring job postings to disclose pay ranges—yet internal disclosure among current employees remains culturally suppressed.

3. Negotiation & Economic Self-Interest

Bargaining Power Erosion

If a colleague or future employer knows your exact compensation, it becomes an anchor point that limits your negotiating range. Revealing $85K when you could command $110K hands the number to the other side of the table.

Salary data asymmetry is a core feature of labor markets: employers benefit when workers don't know what peers earn.

Equity & Fairness Anxiety

People often suspect pay inequity but avoid confirming it. Knowing a peer earns more for the same role creates cognitive dissonance—you must either accept an unfair system or confront it. Many choose avoidance to preserve psychological comfort.

This is especially acute along gender, racial, and age lines, where disparities are statistically common but individually uncomfortable to surface.

4. Social & Cultural Taboos

Money as a Private Category

In many cultures—particularly Anglo-American, East Asian, and Middle Eastern—money is treated as taboo in casual conversation. Discussing salary can violate norms of:

  • Modesty norms — "You shouldn't brag about money."
  • Class sensitivity — Revealing income exposes social class, which many find embarrassing or judgment-inducing.
  • Family obligation pressure — In cultures with strong familial financial interdependence, revealing income invites demands for loans, gifts, or support.
  • Friendship asymmetry — A salary gap can introduce a power dynamic into a peer relationship, shifting it from "equals" to "patron/client."

5. Safety & Practical Concerns

Fraud & Targeting Risk

Salary data, combined with employer name and role, creates a social engineering profile. Phishing attempts, identity theft, and targeted scams become more credible when an attacker knows your income bracket.

Safety in High-Disparity Environments

In regions with extreme wealth inequality, publicly known high earners face elevated risk of kidnapping, theft, extortion, or social targeting. This is a genuine safety consideration, not merely paranoia.

6. The Gender & Equity Dimension

Gender Pay Gap (US, 2024) ~17% Women earn ~83¢ per $1 earned by men
Women Who Avoid Pay Talk ~2× More likely than men to avoid salary conversations at work
Transparency Laws (US States) 23 Requiring salary ranges in job postings (2024)

Women face a double bind: transparency helps close equity gaps, but speaking up about pay is disproportionately penalized as "difficult," "aggressive," or "unprofessional." The social cost of disclosure is gendered.

7. What Actually Encourages Sharing

1

Anonymized Aggregation

Platforms like Glassdoor, Levels.fyi, or Blind let people share salary data without personal attribution, reducing social risk while preserving information value.

2

Legal & Policy Mandates

When transparency is institutionalized (salary bands, public pay scales, posted ranges), the social awkwardness of disclosure evaporates because the information is already public.

3

Trusted Small Groups

People share within high-trust micro-communities—close friends, union members, mentor circles—where the relational safety net absorbs potential judgment or envy.

4

Reframing as Advocacy

When pay transparency is framed as a collective equity tool rather than personal exposure, participation rates increase. The narrative shifts from "What am I worth?" to "What is this role worth?"

Summary: The Hidden Cost Matrix

Reason for SilenceWho Bears the Cost of SharingWho Benefits from Secrecy
Social comparison anxietySpeaker (shame, envy)High earners (status preservation)
Negotiation disadvantageSpeaker (lower future offers)Employers (cheaper labor)
Workplace retaliationSpeaker (career risk)Management (information control)
Cultural taboo / class stigmaSpeaker (social awkwardness)Those already advantaged
Family / relational pressureSpeaker (obligation, jealousy)Relationships seeking equilibrium
Fraud & safety riskSpeaker (personal security)—
Bottom Line

Salary secrecy is not a single cause but a convergence of individual psychology, organizational power, cultural norms, and legal structure. The people who benefit most from silence are rarely the people who suffer most from it. The path to transparency runs through anonymization, legal mandate, and collective reframing—not through asking individuals to simply "just share."

instruction: In D&D, how many attacks can a fighter with two-weapon fighting make at 5th level?
cot:
The user is asking about D&D 5e's Fighter class, specifically the Two-Weapon Fighting feature at 5th level. Let me think through this carefully.

At 5th level, a Fighter has:
- Extra Attack (from the Fighter class at 5th level) - allows 2 attacks with the Attack action
- Two-Weapon Fighting (from the Fighting Style at 1st level) - allows adding ability modifier to damage of the bonus action off-hand attack

The Two-Weapon Fighting rules (PHB p.195):
- When you take the Attack action and attack with a light melee weapon in one hand, you can use a bonus action to attack with a different light melee weapon in the other hand.
- You don't gain the ability to add your ability modifier to the damage of the bonus attack, unless that modifier is negative.
- BUT: If either weapon has the "thrown" property, you can throw it instead of making a melee attack.

The Two-Weapon Fighting fighting style (PHB p.72):
- When you engage in two-weapon fighting, you can add your ability modifier to the damage of the second attack.

So at 5th level, a Fighter with Two-Weapon Fighting:
1. Attack action: 2 attacks (from Extra Attack) with the main-hand light melee weapon
2. Bonus action: 1 attack with the off-hand light melee weapon (because they took the Attack action and attacked with a light melee weapon)

Total: 3 attacks per turn.

Wait, let me be more careful. The Extra Attack feature says "you can make two attacks instead of one when you take the Attack action." So with Extra Attack, you get 2 attacks from the Attack action. Then Two-Weapon Fighting gives you 1 bonus action attack. Total = 3 attacks.

But there's a subtlety: Can you make the bonus action off-hand attack only once per turn, even with Extra Attack? Yes. The bonus action attack is triggered by "when you take the Attack action and attack with a light melee weapon in one hand." You only get one bonus action per turn, so only one off-hand attack regardless of how many main-hand attacks you make.

So the answer is 3 attacks total at 5th level.

Let me also consider: At 11th level, Extra Attack becomes 

I have thought about this long enough; time to give my answer.
html:
Two-Weapon Fighting at Fighter Level 5

A 5th-level Fighter with the Two-Weapon Fighting fighting style makes 3 attacks per turn: two from the Attack action (via Extra Attack) and one from a bonus action (the off-hand light weapon).

Attack Action → 2 Attacks

At 5th level the Fighter gains Extra Attack, so a single Attack action lets you swing your main-hand light melee weapon twice.

Extra Attack (Lv 5)

Bonus Action → 1 Attack

Because you took the Attack action and attacked with a light melee weapon, the Two-Weapon Fighting rule lets you use your bonus action to attack once with your off-hand light melee weapon.

Two-Weapon Fighting (Lv 1 style)

Key Limitation

You only have one bonus action per turn, so regardless of how many main-hand attacks Extra Attack grants, you still get only one off-hand bonus-action attack.

SourceAttacksAction Type
Extra Attack (Fighter Lv 5)2Attack action
Two-Weapon Fighting (Fighting Style)1Bonus action
Total per turn3—

Damage Modifier Reminder

The Two-Weapon Fighting fighting style (chosen at 1st level) lets you add your ability modifier to the damage of the off-hand bonus attack. Without this style, the off-hand attack adds no modifier to damage.

  • Main hand: 2 attacks × (weapon damage + ability modifier)
  • Off hand: 1 attack × (weapon damage + ability modifier) (thanks to the fighting style)
Requirements Checklist
  • Both weapons must be light melee weapons (e.g., shortsword + dagger).
  • You must be holding both weapons (or have one drawn).
  • You must have taken the Attack action and made at least one attack with the main-hand weapon.
  • Two weapons must each be in a separate hand.
Main-hand attacks2Attack action
Off-hand attack1Bonus action
Total attacks3per turn

At 5th level, a Fighter has: - Extra Attack (from the Fighter class at 5th level) - allows 2 attacks with the Attack action - Two-Weapon Fighting (from the Fighting Style at 1st level) - allows adding ability modifier to damage of the bonus action off-hand attack The Two-Weapon Fighting rules (PHB p.195): - When you take the Attack action and attack with a light melee weapon in one hand, you can use a bonus action to attack with a different light melee weapon in the other hand. - You don't gain the ability to add your ability modifier to the damage of the bonus attack, unless that modifier is negative. - BUT: If either weapon has the "thrown" property, you can throw it instead of making a melee attack. The Two-Weapon Fighting fighting style (PHB p.72): - When you engage in two-weapon fighting, you can add your ability modifier to the damage of the second attack. So at 5th level, a Fighter with Two-Weapon Fighting: 1. Attack action: 2 attacks (from Extra Attack) with the main-hand light melee weapon 2. Bonus action: 1 attack with the off-hand light melee weapon (because they took the Attack action and attacked with a light melee weapon) Total: 3 attacks per turn. Wait, let me be more careful. The Extra Attack feature says "you can make two attacks instead of one when you take the Attack action." So with Extra Attack, you get 2 attacks from the Attack action. Then Two-Weapon Fighting gives you 1 bonus action attack. Total = 3 attacks. But there's a subtlety: Can you make the bonus action off-hand attack only once per turn, even with Extra Attack? Yes. The bonus action attack is triggered by "when you take the Attack action and attack with a light melee weapon in one hand." You only get one bonus action per turn, so only one off-hand attack regardless of how many main-hand attacks you make. So the answer is 3 attacks total at 5th level. A 5th-level Fighter with the Two-Weapon Fighting fighting style makes 3 attacks per turn: two from the Attack action (via Extra Attack) and one from a bonus action (the off-hand light weapon).
